title: Consider an unnormalized relation Student_Marks(Rollno, Name, Subject, Marks) where a student appears in multiple rows, one per subject. Normalize it step by step up to 3NF, clearly stating the functional dependencies you have assumed.
chunks: Functional Dependencies (FDs) Assumed FDs based on logic: FD1: Rollno → Name (A student has one name) FD2: Rollno, Subject → Marks (A specific student's marks in a specific subject) The primary key for the unnormalized relation is (Rollno, Subject) . Step 1: 1NF to 2NF In the original relation, Name depends ONLY on Rollno , which is a part of the primary key. This is a Partial Dependency . We decompose to eliminate it: Student ( Rollno , Name) Performance ( Rollno, Subject , Marks) Step 2: 2NF to 3NF In the new tables, there are no non-key attributes depending on other non-key attributes (no transitive dependencies). Therefore, the tables are already in 3NF .
subject: dbms

title: A hostel management register stores the occupants of each room as shown in the table below. Redesign this data into a table that satisfies 1NF.
chunks: Problem Context In the unnormalized table, a single cell (like "Occupants") contains multiple values (e.g., "Alice, Bob"), which violates the atomicity rule of 1NF. 1NF Solution To convert to 1NF, we eliminate repeating groups by ensuring each cell holds only a single, atomic value. We duplicate the room number for each occupant. Room_No Occupant 101 Alice 101 Bob 102 Charlie Now, the primary key becomes the composite key (Room_No, Occupant) .
subject: dbms

title: The table below has the composite key (StudentID, SubjectID). Identify the partial dependencies present and decompose the table into 2NF.
chunks: Identifying Partial Dependencies Suppose the relation is R(StudentID, SubjectID, StudentName, Grade) . The primary key is (StudentID, SubjectID) . StudentID → StudentName (StudentName depends only on part of the key) — Partial Dependency StudentID, SubjectID → Grade (Grade depends on the whole key) — Full Dependency Decomposition into 2NF We split the table to remove the partial dependency: Student ( StudentID , StudentName) Enrollment ( StudentID, SubjectID , Grade) Both tables are now in 2NF as all non-prime attributes fully depend on their respective primary keys.
subject: dbms

title: The table below has EmployeeID as its primary key. Show that it violates 3NF, and decompose it into a set of tables that satisfy 3NF.
chunks: Violation of 3NF Consider Employee(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID is the primary key. Functional Dependencies: 1. EmpID → DeptID 2. DeptID → DeptName Because EmpID → DeptName through DeptID , this is a Transitive Dependency . 3NF forbids non-prime attributes depending on other non-prime attributes. Decomposition into 3NF We decompose the relation to separate the department details: Employee ( EmpID , Name, DeptID ) Department ( DeptID , DeptName)
subject: dbms

title: In the table below, each mentor teaches only one subject. Given that the candidate keys of this table are (StudentID, Subject) and (StudentID, Mentor), check whether it satisfies BCNF. If it does not, decompose it into BCNF.
chunks: Checking BCNF Relation: R(StudentID, Subject, Mentor) FDs: {StudentID, Subject} → Mentor , and Mentor → Subject (each mentor teaches one subject). Because Mentor → Subject exists, but Mentor is not a super key , the table violates BCNF (even though it is in 3NF since Subject is a prime attribute). BCNF Decomposition We must pull the violating determinant out into its own table: Mentor_Subject ( Mentor , Subject) Student_Mentor ( StudentID, Mentor ) Now all determinants are candidate keys.
subject: dbms

title: The table below stores a student's hobbies and the languages they know together, forcing every combination to be listed. Explain why this table is not in 4NF, and decompose it into a form that satisfies 4NF.
chunks: Violation of 4NF Relation: R(StudentID, Hobby, Language) A student's hobbies are completely independent of the languages they speak. This creates two Multi-Valued Dependencies (MVDs) : StudentID ⟶ Hobby and StudentID ⟶ Language . Storing them together forces a Cartesian product (e.g., 2 hobbies × 3 languages = 6 rows for one student). Since 4NF forbids non-trivial MVDs, this violates 4NF. 4NF Decomposition Split into two tables to eliminate the Cartesian product: Student_Hobby ( StudentID, Hobby ) Student_Language ( StudentID, Language )
subject: dbms

title: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with the functional dependency set F = {A -> B, BC -> D, D -> E}, compute the closure of {A, C} and state whether {A, C} is a candidate key of R.
chunks: Computing {A, C} + Start with the base set: {A, C} Using A → B , add B. The set becomes {A, B, C} Using BC → D (we have both B and C), add D. The set becomes {A, B, C, D} Using D → E , add E. The set becomes {A, B, C, D, E} Conclusion Since the closure of {A, C} contains all the attributes of the relation R, {A, C} is a super key . Assuming no proper subset of {A, C} can determine all attributes, {A, C} is a Candidate Key .
subject: dbms

title: Consider the relation Student_Course(Roll_No, Course_ID, Course_Name, Instructor) with the functional dependencies {Roll_No, Course_ID} -> Instructor, and Course_ID -> Course_Name. Identify the partial dependency present, show why the relation is not in 2NF, and decompose it into 2NF.
chunks: Analysis Primary Key: (Roll_No, Course_ID) The FD Course_ID → Course_Name is a Partial Dependency because Course_Name depends only on a part of the primary key (Course_ID), violating 2NF. 2NF Decomposition Course ( Course_ID , Course_Name) Student_Course ( Roll_No, Course_ID , Instructor) Now, both relations are in 2NF.
subject: dbms

title: Consider the relation Employee(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name, Dept_Location) with the functional dependencies Emp_ID -> Emp_Name, Dept_ID and Dept_ID -> Dept_Name, Dept_Location. Show that this relation is in 2NF but violates 3NF, and decompose it into 3NF.
chunks: Analysis Primary Key: Emp_ID . Since the key is a single attribute, there are no partial dependencies, so it is in 2NF . However, the FD Dept_ID → Dept_Name, Dept_Location creates a Transitive Dependency (Emp_ID → Dept_ID → Dept_Name). This violates 3NF. 3NF Decomposition Employee ( Emp_ID , Emp_Name, Dept_ID ) Department ( Dept_ID , Dept_Name, Dept_Location)
subject: dbms

title: Consider the relation R(Student, Subject, Teacher) with the functional dependencies {Student, Subject} -> Teacher and Teacher -> Subject. Determine whether R is in BCNF. If it is not, decompose it into a set of relations that are in BCNF.
chunks: Analysis Candidate Keys: (Student, Subject) and (Student, Teacher) . For the FD Teacher → Subject , Teacher is a determinant but not a super key . Therefore, R violates BCNF. BCNF Decomposition Teach_Subj ( Teacher , Subject) Stud_Teach ( Student, Teacher ) Both tables are now strictly in BCNF.
subject: dbms

title: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D) with the functional dependency set F = {AB -> C, C -> D, D -> A}, find all the candidate keys of R and state the highest normal form it satisfies.
chunks: Candidate Keys {A, B} + = {A, B, C, D} {B, C} + = {A, B, C, D} (since C → D and D → A) {B, D} + = {A, B, C, D} (since D → A and AB → C) The candidate keys are AB, BC, and BD . All attributes are prime attributes except none (every attribute is part of at least one candidate key). Highest Normal Form Because there are no non-prime attributes, the relation is automatically in 3NF . However, check BCNF: The FD C → D has determinant C, which is not a super key. Thus, it violates BCNF. The highest normal form is 3NF .
subject: dbms

title: What is an RDBMS? How does it differ from a DBMS?
chunks: Feature DBMS RDBMS Data Storage Stores data as files. Stores data in tabular form (rows and columns). Relationships Does not support relationships easily. Supports complex relationships using foreign keys.
subject: dbms

title: Explain how entities and relationships of the E-R model are represented in a relational database.
chunks: Strong Entities: Represented as standalone tables. Relationships (1:N): The primary key of the '1' side is added as a foreign key to the 'N' side table. Relationships (M:N): Handled by creating a new junction table containing the primary keys of both entities.
subject: dbms

title: Consider the relational schema Student(sid, sname), Course(cid, cname), Enrollment(sid, cid). Write relational algebra expressions.
chunks: i. Names of students enrolled in 'DBMS' π sname ( σ cname='DBMS' (Student ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ Course) ) ii. Courses where 'Alice' is enrolled π cname ( σ sname='Alice' (Course ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ Student) )
subject: dbms

title: What are the derived operations of relational algebra? Explain Join, Intersection and Division with examples.
chunks: Derived operations are built using fundamental operations (σ, π, ×, ∪, -). Intersection (∩): Returns tuples existing in both relations. Join (⨝): A cartesian product followed by a selection. Division (÷): Used for queries involving the word "every" (e.g., students who took all courses).
subject: dbms

title: Distinguish between relational algebra and relational calculus.
chunks: Relational Algebra Relational Calculus Procedural query language. Non-procedural (declarative) query language. Specifies what data is required and how to retrieve it. Specifies what data is required without specifying how to retrieve it.
subject: dbms

title: What is the degree and cardinality of a relation?
chunks: Degree: The number of attributes (columns) in a relation. Cardinality: The number of tuples (rows) in a relation.
subject: dbms

title: What is domain relational calculus? Give an example.
chunks: Domain Relational Calculus (DRC) is a declarative query language where variables represent single attribute values (domains). Syntax: { <x1, x2, ..., xn> | P(x1, x2, ..., xn) } Example: { <N> | ∃ I, A, C ( <I, N, A, C> ∈ Student ∧ A > 20 ) }
subject: dbms

title: Explain DDL, DML, DCL and TCL commands with one example of each.
chunks: DDL: Defines structure (e.g., CREATE TABLE ). DML: Manages data (e.g., INSERT INTO ). DCL: Manages security (e.g., GRANT ). TCL: Manages transactions (e.g., COMMIT ).
subject: dbms

title: What is the use of CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE commands?
chunks: CREATE: Used to create new tables/objects. ALTER: Used to modify an existing table structure (add/drop columns). DROP: Deletes an entire table and its structure. TRUNCATE: Deletes all rows rapidly, but keeps the structure intact.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the DML commands INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT.
chunks: INSERT: Adds new rows. UPDATE: Modifies existing rows. DELETE: Removes specific rows. SELECT: Retrieves data from the database.
subject: dbms

title: What is the purpose of GRANT and REVOKE commands in SQL?
chunks: GRANT and REVOKE belong to the DCL (Data Control Language) category. They are used to manage database security by controlling user privileges. GRANT: Gives a user or role specific privileges on database objects. Example: GRANT SELECT ON Employees TO user_alice; REVOKE: Removes previously granted privileges. Example: REVOKE SELECT ON Employees FROM user_alice;
subject: dbms

title: Explain COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT with a suitable example.
chunks: These are TCL (Transaction Control Language) commands used to manage transactions. COMMIT: Permanently saves all changes made during the current transaction. ROLLBACK: Undoes all changes made in the current transaction. SAVEPOINT: Creates a checkpoint within a transaction to rollback to later. BEGIN; UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE id = 1; SAVEPOINT SP1; UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE id = 2; ROLLBACK TO SP1; -- Undoes the second update COMMIT; -- Permanently saves the first update
subject: dbms

title: What is a join? Explain the different types of joins, inner, left outer, right outer and full outer, with examples.
chunks: A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column. Inner Join Returns only rows with matching values in both tables. SELECT A.Name, B.Dept FROM Emp A INNER JOIN Dept B ON A.DeptID = B.DeptID; Outer Joins Left Outer: Returns all rows from the left table, and matched rows from the right. Right Outer: Returns all rows from the right table, and matched rows from the left. Full Outer: Returns all rows when there is a match in either table.
subject: dbms

title: Differentiate between an equi join and a natural join, with an example of each.
chunks: Equi Join Natural Join Explicitly uses the equality operator ( = ) in the ON clause. Implicitly matches on all columns that have the same name . No ON clause is used. Output contains duplicate matching columns. Output automatically removes duplicate matching columns. SELECT * FROM Emp JOIN Dept ON Emp.DeptID = Dept.DeptID; SELECT * FROM Emp NATURAL JOIN Dept;
subject: dbms

title: What is a self join? What is a cross join? Explain with examples.
chunks: Self Join A table is joined with itself using aliases. SELECT E.Name AS Employee, M.Name AS Manager FROM Employee E JOIN Employee M ON E.ManagerID = M.EmpID; Cross Join Produces the Cartesian Product of two tables (every row matched with every row). SELECT T.Name, C.RoomNo FROM Teachers T CROSS JOIN Classrooms C;
subject: dbms

title: Explain the aggregate functions available in SQL, COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX and MIN, giving an example of each.
chunks: Aggregate functions perform a calculation on a set of values and return a single summarizing value. COUNT(): Returns the number of rows. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Employees; SUM(): Returns the total sum of a column. SELECT SUM(Salary) FROM Employees; AVG(): Returns the average value. SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employees; MAX() / MIN(): Returns the largest / smallest value. SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees;
subject: dbms

title: What is the purpose of the GROUP BY clause? Explain with a suitable query.
chunks: The GROUP BY clause is used to arrange identical data into groups. It is typically used in conjunction with aggregate functions (COUNT, MAX, MIN, SUM, AVG). Scenario: Find the total number of employees in each department. SELECT DeptID, COUNT(EmpID) AS TotalEmployees FROM Employee GROUP BY DeptID;
subject: dbms

title: How is the HAVING clause different from the WHERE clause? Justify with an example.
chunks: WHERE Clause HAVING Clause Filters individual rows before grouping. Filters groups after grouping. Cannot contain aggregate functions. Can contain aggregate functions. Example SELECT DeptID, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee WHERE HireDate > '2020-01-01' -- Filters rows first GROUP BY DeptID HAVING AVG(Salary) > 50000; -- Filters groups
subject: dbms

title: Explain the use of the ORDER BY clause with an example.
chunks: The ORDER BY clause is used to sort the result set of a query in either ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order. Example: SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee ORDER BY Salary DESC;
subject: dbms

title: What are nested queries? Why are they used? Explain with a suitable example.
chunks: A nested query (subquery) is a query embedded within another query. They are used to break down complex queries into isolated steps. Scenario: Find employees who earn a salary greater than the average salary. SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee);
subject: dbms

title: What is a correlated subquery? How is it different from a simple subquery?
chunks: Simple Subquery Correlated Subquery Executes completely independent of the outer query. Depends on the outer query for its values. Executes exactly once for the entire outer query. Executes repeatedly , once for every row processed by the outer query. Example (Correlated) SELECT Name, Salary FROM Employee E1 WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employee E2 WHERE E1.DeptID = E2.DeptID);
subject: dbms

title: Explain the use of IN, EXISTS, ANY and ALL operators in a nested query.
chunks: IN: Checks if a value matches any value in a list or subquery result. WHERE DeptID IN (SELECT DeptID FROM Departments) EXISTS: Evaluates to TRUE if the subquery returns one or more records. WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Orders.CustID = Customers.ID) ANY (or SOME): Compares a value to each value in a list and evaluates to TRUE if any comparison is true. WHERE Salary > ANY (SELECT Salary FROM IT_Dept) ALL: Evaluates to TRUE only if the comparison is true for all values in the list. WHERE Salary > ALL (SELECT Salary FROM Interns)
subject: dbms

title: What is a view? What are its advantages?
chunks: A View is a virtual table based on the result-set of an SQL statement. It contains rows and columns, just like a real table, but holds no data of its own. Advantages Security: Restricts access to specific rows/columns of a table. Simplicity: Hides complex joins and calculations into a single virtual table. Data Independence: Insulates applications from changes in base table structures.
subject: dbms

title: Differentiate between a simple view and a materialized view.
chunks: Simple View Materialized View Virtual table; does not store data physically. Stores the actual result data physically on disk. Query is executed every time the view is accessed. Data is pre-computed, providing much faster read access. Always shows up-to-date real-time data. Needs to be refreshed periodically to show updated data.
subject: dbms

title: Can every view be updated? Explain the limitations of an updatable view with an example.
chunks: No , not all views can be updated. A view is updatable only if the DBMS can unambiguously trace the update back to the underlying base table rows. Limitations (Cannot Update If:) It contains aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX). It contains GROUP BY or HAVING clauses. It is built using multiple tables (Joins), depending on the DBMS. It uses the DISTINCT keyword. Example A view CREATE VIEW Dept_Salaries AS SELECT DeptID, AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY DeptID; cannot be updated because an update to an average salary cannot be mapped to individual employees.
subject: dbms

title: Explain generalization, specialization and aggregation in the Extended E-R model.
chunks: Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from an entity type based on distinguishing characteristics. Example: An Employee can be specialized into Hourly_Emp and Salaried_Emp . Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse of specialization. Extracting shared characteristics from multiple entity types to create a generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck generalized into Vehicle . Aggregation Treating a relationship between entities as a single abstract entity, allowing relationships to participate in other relationships. Example: A Project and Employee have a Works_On relationship. A Manager manages the entire Works_On relationship, treating it as one aggregated entity.
subject: dbms

title: What is decomposition? Explain the concepts of lossless-join and dependency-preserving decomposition.
chunks: Decomposition is the process of breaking down a large, poorly-designed relation into two or more smaller relations to eliminate redundancy and anomalies. Lossless-Join Decomposition A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining R1 and R2 back together using a Natural Join yields the exact original relation R, without generating spurious (fake) tuples. Condition: The common attributes must be a candidate key for at least one of the decomposed relations (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 ). Dependency-Preserving Decomposition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if all original functional dependencies can be checked and enforced using only the decomposed relations, without needing to join them back together.
subject: dbms

title: How is decomposition related to normalization? Explain with a small example.
chunks: Normalization uses Decomposition as its primary mechanism. When a relation violates a normal form, we decompose it into smaller relations that satisfy the normal form. Example Suppose a relation R(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID → EmpName, DeptID and DeptID → DeptName . This violates 3NF due to the transitive dependency ( EmpID → DeptID → DeptName ). Normalization Process: We decompose R into two relations to remove the redundancy: 1. Employee(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID) 2. Department(DeptID, DeptName) This decomposition is both lossless-join (because DeptID is a primary key in Department) and dependency-preserving.
subject: dbms

title: Compare relational algebra with SQL as two different ways of expressing the same query.
chunks: Feature Relational Algebra SQL Nature Theoretical, mathematical foundation. Procedural. Practical, commercial language. Declarative. Selection (Rows) σ condition (Table) WHERE condition Projection (Columns) π col1, col2 (Table) SELECT col1, col2 Joins Table1 ⨝ Table2 Table1 JOIN Table2 Duplicates Automatically removes duplicates (set semantics). Retains duplicates by default (bag semantics); requires DISTINCT to remove.
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to display the names of students who are enrolled in the course 'DBMS'.
chunks: Assuming the standard schema: Student(sid, sname) , Course(cid, cname) , Enrollment(sid, cid) . SELECT s.sname FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid WHERE c.cname = 'DBMS'; Alternative (Using Subqueries) SELECT sname FROM Student WHERE sid IN ( SELECT sid FROM Enrollment WHERE cid IN ( SELECT cid FROM Course WHERE cname = 'DBMS' ) );
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to display, course-wise, how many students have enrolled in each course.
chunks: Using the standard schema: Course(cid, cname) , Enrollment(sid, cid) . SELECT c.cname, COUNT(e.sid) AS NumberOfStudents FROM Course c JOIN Enrollment e ON c.cid = e.cid GROUP BY c.cid, c.cname;
subject: dbms

title: Write a query using HAVING to display students who are enrolled in more than 3 courses.
chunks: SELECT s.sname, COUNT(e.cid) AS EnrolledCourses FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid GROUP BY s.sid, s.sname HAVING COUNT(e.cid) > 3;
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to display the student name along with the names of the courses they have opted for, using a suitable join.
chunks: We use a standard INNER JOIN to connect the three tables. SELECT s.sname, c.cname FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid;
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to find students who have not enrolled in any course so far.
chunks: Using LEFT JOIN SELECT s.sname FROM Student s LEFT JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid WHERE e.cid IS NULL; Using NOT EXISTS SELECT sname FROM Student s WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Enrollment e WHERE e.sid = s.sid );
subject: dbms

title: Write a nested query to find the student(s) who scored the highest marks in the course 'DBMS'.
chunks: Assuming Enrollment(sid, cid, marks) . SELECT s.sname, e.marks FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid WHERE c.cname = 'DBMS' AND e.marks = ( SELECT MAX(e2.marks) FROM Enrollment e2 JOIN Course c2 ON e2.cid = c2.cid WHERE c2.cname = 'DBMS' );
subject: dbms

title: Create a view that shows the student name, course name and marks for every enrollment record.
chunks: CREATE VIEW Student_Grades AS SELECT s.sname, c.cname, e.marks FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e ON s.sid = e.sid JOIN Course c ON e.cid = c.cid; You can then query this view like a regular table: SELECT * FROM Student_Grades;
subject: dbms

title: Write a relational algebra expression to retrieve the names of students enrolled in the course 'DBMS'.
chunks: Relational Algebra: π sname ( Student ⨝ Enrollment ⨝ σ cname='DBMS' (Course) ) Breakdown: Select only the course where cname is 'DBMS' (σ). Natural Join (⨝) the result with Enrollment and Student. Project (π) only the student name (sname).
subject: dbms

title: Using the division operation of relational algebra, write an expression to find students who are enrolled in every course offered.
chunks: The division operator ( ÷ ) is used specifically for queries involving "every" or "all". Expression: π sid (Enrollment) ÷ π cid (Course) To get the student names, we natural join this result with the Student table: π sname ( Student ⨝ (π sid, cid (Enrollment) ÷ π cid (Course)) )
subject: dbms

title: Write a correlated subquery to list students who have scored more than the average marks obtained in their respective course.
chunks: SELECT s.sname, e1.cid, e1.marks FROM Student s JOIN Enrollment e1 ON s.sid = e1.sid WHERE e1.marks > ( SELECT AVG(e2.marks) FROM Enrollment e2 WHERE e1.cid = e2.cid ); The inner query recalculates the average marks dynamically for every row of the outer query, matching the cid .
subject: dbms

title: What is the use of CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE commands? Why are DDL statements said to be auto-committed?
chunks: CREATE TABLE is used to create a new table in the database. ALTER TABLE is used to add, delete, or modify columns in an existing table. DROP TABLE is used to delete an existing table completely (including its structure and data). DDL statements are auto-committed because they alter the database schema directly and cannot be rolled back in most RDBMS like MySQL and Oracle.
subject: dbms

title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for a Library_Book table having Book_ID, Title, Author, Price and Published_Date, choosing appropriate data types.
chunks: CREATE TABLE Library_Book ( Book_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Title VARCHAR(100), Author VARCHAR(50), Price DECIMAL(8,2), Published_Date DATE );
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to add a column Email of type VARCHAR(40) to the Student table.
chunks: ALTER TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(40);

title: Write a query to change the data type of the Fees column in the Student table to DECIMAL(10,2).
chunks: ALTER TABLE Student MODIFY Fees DECIMAL(10,2);
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to rename the Course column of the Student table as Program.
chunks: ALTER TABLE Student RENAME COLUMN Course TO Program; (Note: Syntax varies slightly between RDBMS. In older MySQL versions, CHANGE Course Program VARCHAR(...) is used).
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to rename the table Student to Student_Info.
chunks: ALTER TABLE Student RENAME TO Student_Info; Alternatively: RENAME TABLE Student TO Student_Info;

title: Using CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT, write a query to create a backup table Student_Backup from the Student table.
chunks: CREATE TABLE Student_Backup AS SELECT * FROM Student;
subject: dbms

title: Give the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP commands.
chunks: DELETE is a DML command used to remove specific rows based on a WHERE clause. It can be rolled back. TRUNCATE is a DDL command that removes all rows from a table quickly by deallocating the pages. It cannot be rolled back and resets identity columns. DROP is a DDL command that completely deletes the table structure and its data from the database.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the five constraints NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK, giving an example of each.
chunks: NOT NULL : Ensures a column cannot have a NULL value. Ex: Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE : Ensures all values in a column are distinct. Ex: Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE PRIMARY KEY : Uniquely identifies each record. It is NOT NULL + UNIQUE. Ex: ID INT PRIMARY KEY FOREIGN KEY : Ensures referential integrity by linking to a primary key in another table. Ex: FOREIGN KEY (DeptID) REFERENCES Dept(ID) CHECK : Ensures values in a column satisfy a specific condition. Ex: Age INT CHECK (Age >= 18)
subject: dbms

title: What is the difference between a column-level and a table-level constraint? When is a table-level constraint compulsory?
chunks: Column-level constraints are defined immediately after the data type of a column. Table-level constraints are defined at the end of the table creation and can span multiple columns. A table-level constraint is compulsory when defining a composite key (a constraint that involves more than one column).
subject: dbms

title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Department(Dept_ID, Dept_Name), keeping Dept_ID as the primary key.
chunks: CREATE TABLE Department ( Dept_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Dept_Name VARCHAR(50) );
subject: dbms

title: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for Employee(Emp_ID, Name, Email, Dept_ID, Salary), where Emp_ID is the primary key, Name cannot be left blank and Email must be unique.
chunks: CREATE TABLE Employee ( Emp_ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, Email VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE, Dept_ID INT, Salary DECIMAL(10,2) );
subject: dbms

title: Using ALTER TABLE, add a foreign key on Employee.Dept_ID referencing Department.Dept_ID.
chunks: ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT fk_dept FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID);
subject: dbms

title: Using ALTER TABLE, put a check constraint on the Employee table so that Salary is always greater than zero.
chunks: ALTER TABLE Employee ADD CONSTRAINT chk_salary CHECK (Salary > 0);
subject: dbms

title: A table can have more than one UNIQUE constraint but only one PRIMARY KEY. Justify why this is so.
chunks: A Primary Key is strictly designed to be the single, definitive row identifier used by the database engine to organize and index the physical storage (e.g. clustered index). There can only be one physical ordering. However, multiple columns may have naturally unique data (like an Email or Phone number), which is why multiple UNIQUE constraints are permitted to enforce business rules.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the numeric functions ROUND, TRUNCATE, CEIL, FLOOR, ABS, MOD, POWER and SQRT, giving an example of each.
chunks: ROUND(n, d) : Rounds n to d decimal places. ROUND(3.456, 2) → 3.46 TRUNCATE(n, d) : Cuts off n at d decimal places without rounding. TRUNCATE(3.456, 2) → 3.45 CEIL(n) : Returns the smallest integer ≥ n . CEIL(3.14) → 4 FLOOR(n) : Returns the largest integer ≤ n . FLOOR(3.8) → 3 ABS(n) : Returns the absolute (positive) value. ABS(-5) → 5 MOD(x, y) : Returns the remainder of x/y. MOD(10, 3) → 1 POWER(x, y) : Returns x raised to power y. POWER(2, 3) → 8 SQRT(n) : Returns the square root. SQRT(16) → 4
subject: dbms

title: Round off 78.3456 to 2 decimal places using ROUND, and also truncate it to 2 decimal places using TRUNCATE. Why do the two results come out different?
chunks: SELECT ROUND(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.35 SELECT TRUNCATE(78.3456, 2); -- Result: 78.34 Reason : ROUND evaluates the third decimal digit (5) and mathematically rounds up. TRUNCATE simply drops all digits after the 2nd decimal place without any mathematical evaluation.
subject: dbms

title: Write a query on PRODUCT_MAST to display each Product_Name along with its Price rounded to the nearest whole number.
chunks: SELECT Product_Name, ROUND(Price, 0) AS Rounded_Price FROM PRODUCT_MAST;

title: Find the remainder when 29 is divided by 4 using MOD, and use the same function to check whether 29 is odd or even.
chunks: -- Find remainder SELECT MOD(29, 4); -- Check if odd/even (if remainder is 1, it is odd) SELECT MOD(29, 2);
subject: dbms

title: Find the square of 12 using POWER and the square root of 144 using SQRT.
chunks: SELECT POWER(12, 2) AS Square, SQRT(144) AS Root;

title: Explain the date functions CURDATE, DATEDIFF, DATE_ADD/DATE_SUB and DATE_FORMAT, giving an example of each.
chunks: CURDATE() : Returns the current system date. Ex: SELECT CURDATE(); DATEDIFF(date1, date2) : Returns the number of days between two dates. Ex: SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-10-10', '2023-10-01'); → 9 DATE_ADD(date, INTERVAL expr unit) : Adds a time interval to a date. Ex: SELECT DATE_ADD('2023-01-01', INTERVAL 5 DAY); DATE_FORMAT(date, format) : Formats a date string. Ex: SELECT DATE_FORMAT(CURDATE(), '%Y-%m-%d');
subject: dbms

title: Explain the string functions CONCAT, UPPER/LOWER, LENGTH, SUBSTRING and TRIM/REPLACE, giving an example of each.
chunks: CONCAT(s1, s2) : Joins two or more strings. Ex: CONCAT('Data', 'base') → 'Database' UPPER(s) / LOWER(s) : Converts a string to all uppercase or lowercase. Ex: UPPER('sql') → 'SQL' LENGTH(s) : Returns the number of characters in a string. Ex: LENGTH('DBMS') → 4 SUBSTRING(s, start, len) : Extracts a part of a string. Ex: SUBSTRING('Database', 1, 4) → 'Data' TRIM(s) : Removes leading and trailing spaces. Ex: TRIM(' SQL ') → 'SQL' REPLACE(s, old, new) : Replaces all occurrences of a substring. Ex: REPLACE('DBMS', 'M', 'B') → 'DBBS'

title: Using DATEDIFF, find the number of days between '2023-01-01' and '2023-12-31'.
chunks: SELECT DATEDIFF('2023-12-31', '2023-01-01') AS Days_Difference; (Note: Syntax may vary slightly by DBMS. In MySQL, it returns 364.)

title: Using DATE_ADD, add 45 days to the date '2024-02-01'.

chunks: SELECT YEAR('2025-03-22') AS Year, MONTH('2025-03-22') AS Month; Alternatively, using DATE_FORMAT in MySQL: SELECT DATE_FORMAT('2025-03-22', '%Y-%m');

title: Write a query on the STUDENT table that displays the full name of every student by joining First_Name and Last_Name with a space in between.
chunks: SELECT CONCAT(First_Name, ' ', Last_Name) AS Full_Name FROM STUDENT;

title: Find the length of the string 'Normalization', and separately extract its first six characters using SUBSTRING.
chunks: SELECT LENGTH('Normalization') AS Str_Length, SUBSTRING('Normalization', 1, 6) AS Extracted_Str;

title: Explain UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and MINUS/EXCEPT with an example of each. What condition must both the SELECT statements satisfy before these operators can be applied?
chunks: Set Operators: UNION : Combines results of two queries, removing duplicates. UNION ALL : Combines results of two queries, keeping all duplicates. INTERSECT : Returns only the rows that appear in both queries. MINUS / EXCEPT : Returns rows from the first query that are not present in the second. Condition for application (Union Compatibility): Both SELECT statements must have the same number of columns. The corresponding columns must have compatible data types in the same order.
subject: dbms

title: Write a query to list every student who is a member of CLUB_CODING or CLUB_MUSIC or both, with no name repeated.
chunks: SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING UNION SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC;

title: Write a query that lists all the rows of CLUB_CODING and CLUB_MUSIC together without removing duplicate names.
chunks: SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING UNION ALL SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC;

title: Write a query to find students who are members of both CLUB_CODING and CLUB_MUSIC.
chunks: SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING INTERSECT SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC;

title: Write a query to find students who are in CLUB_CODING but not in CLUB_MUSIC. Does the order of the two tables in this query matter? Explain.
chunks: SELECT Name FROM CLUB_CODING EXCEPT -- (or MINUS in Oracle) SELECT Name FROM CLUB_MUSIC; Yes, the order matters. A EXCEPT B returns elements in A that are not in B. B EXCEPT A would return students in CLUB_MUSIC who are not in CLUB_CODING.
subject: dbms

title: What is a transaction? Explain the ACID properties with the help of a bank transfer example.
chunks: A transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more SQL statements that must be executed entirely or not at all. ACID Properties (Bank Transfer Example: A to B): Atomicity : "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back. Consistency : The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction. Isolation : Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway. Durability : Once the transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and will survive system crashes. Transaction State Diagram
subject: dbms

title: Explain COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT with a suitable example on the ACCOUNT table.
chunks: COMMIT : Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently. ROLLBACK : Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit. SAVEPOINT : Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction. START TRANSACTION; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A101'; SAVEPOINT step1; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; -- If something goes wrong here: ROLLBACK TO step1; -- Undoes only the A102 update COMMIT; -- Saves the final state
subject: dbms

title: Write a transaction that transfers Rs. 3000 from account A102 to account A103, placing a SAVEPOINT just before the transfer, and finally commit it.
chunks: START TRANSACTION; SAVEPOINT before_transfer; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A103'; COMMIT;
subject: dbms

title: Using a searched CASE statement, classify each account's Balance as 'High' if it is 25000 or more, 'Medium' if it is 15000 or more, and 'Low' otherwise.
chunks: SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, CASE WHEN Balance >= 25000 THEN 'High' WHEN Balance >= 15000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END AS Balance_Category FROM ACCOUNT;
subject: dbms

title: Write a query using IF() that marks accounts with Balance below 15000 as 'Low Balance Alert' and the rest as 'OK'.
chunks: SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, IF(Balance < 15000, 'Low Balance Alert', 'OK') AS Status FROM ACCOUNT;
subject: dbms

title: Write a query using COALESCE() that displays the Nominee_Name column, showing 'Not Registered' wherever this value is missing.
chunks: SELECT Acc_No, Name, COALESCE(Nominee_Name, 'Not Registered') AS Nominee FROM ACCOUNT;
subject: dbms

title: In one or two lines each, state the purpose of a stored procedure, a sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL), a cursor and a trigger.
chunks: Stored Procedure : A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine. Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT) : Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys. Cursor : A database object used to retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure. Trigger : A special type of stored procedure that automatically executes (fires) in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table.
subject: dbms

title: What is the difference between a BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger? What do the keywords NEW and OLD refer to inside a trigger?
chunks: BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data). AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables). NEW refers to the incoming data (being inserted or updated). OLD refers to the existing data in the table before the operation (being updated or deleted).
subject: dbms

title: What is the purpose of exception handling in a stored procedure? Briefly explain DECLARE ... HANDLER and the SIGNAL statement.
chunks: Exception handling ensures that if an error occurs during execution, the stored procedure can catch it and gracefully handle it (e.g., rolling back a transaction) instead of crashing. DECLARE ... HANDLER : Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION ). SIGNAL : Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.
subject: dbms

title: Define a transaction. Mention the two ways in which a transaction can terminate.
chunks: A transaction is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more operations (such as read, write, or update). It executes as an indivisible unit to preserve database consistency. A transaction terminates in two ways: Commit: The transaction completes successfully, making all its modifications permanent and durable on disk. Abort (Rollback): The transaction terminates abnormally; all partial changes are undone, returning the database to its pre-transaction state.
subject: dbms

title: Three transactions are running such that T1 waits for a lock held by T2, T2 waits for a lock held by T3, and T3 waits for a lock held by T1. Draw the wait-for graph and state whether a deadlock exists.
chunks: A Wait-For Graph (WFG) is a directed graph where vertices represent active transactions and directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ is waiting for a lock held by $T_j$. Deadlock Status: Yes, a deadlock exists . The wait-for graph contains the directed cycle $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3 \to T_1$. In concurrency control, a directed cycle in a WFG is a necessary and sufficient condition for deadlock.
subject: dbms

title: What is meant by a recoverable schedule?
chunks: A schedule $S$ is recoverable if, for every pair of transactions $T_i$ and $T_j$ where $T_j$ reads a data item previously written by $T_i$, the commit operation of $T_i$ precedes the commit operation of $T_j$ ($Commit(T_i) < Commit(T_j)$). Significance: Prevents dirty read commits. If $T_i$ aborts, $T_j$ can also be safely rolled back because it has not yet committed. Database Invariant: Commercial DBMSs mandate recoverable schedules to guarantee atomicity and durability during crashes.
subject: dbms

title: Define deadlock and state any two conditions that are necessary for it to occur.
chunks: A deadlock is an execution state where two or more concurrent transactions are permanently blocked because each holds a lock on a data item that another requires, and none can proceed without releasing locks. Two necessary conditions for deadlock are: Mutual Exclusion: A resource is held in an exclusive, non-shareable mode (such as an $X$-lock). Hold and Wait: A transaction holds granted resources while requesting additional resources held by other transactions.
subject: dbms

title: What is a checkpoint in a DBMS? State its purpose in recovery.
chunks: A checkpoint is a synchronization record written to the log during normal operation after flushing all modified buffer blocks (dirty pages) from volatile memory to stable disk storage. Purpose in recovery: Bounds Log Scan: Limits how far back the recovery manager must scan the log during crash restart, eliminating the need to process the log from the very beginning. Reduces Redo Work: Transactions committed prior to the checkpoint already have their updates safely on disk, significantly shortening system recovery downtime.
subject: dbms

title: Differentiate between clustered and non-clustered indexes.
chunks: The key differences between clustered and non-clustered indexes are: Physical Ordering: A clustered index dictates the physical sorting order of actual table rows on disk (only one clustered index per table). A non-clustered index maintains an independent logical order without rearranging physical rows. Leaf Node Content: Leaf nodes of a clustered index contain the actual data records. In a non-clustered index, leaf nodes contain index keys and row pointers (RID / primary key) to data records.
subject: dbms

title: What is a fact table and a dimension table in a data warehouse?
chunks: In data warehouse dimensional modeling (e.g., star schema): Fact Table: The central table containing quantitative numerical measurements (metrics) of a business process (e.g., units_sold , total_amount ) along with foreign keys referencing related dimension tables. Dimension Table: Surrounding companion tables containing descriptive contextual attributes (e.g., customer names, store locations, calendar quarters) used for filtering, grouping, and slicing analytical queries.
subject: dbms

title: Draw the state diagram of a transaction and explain each of its states.
chunks: During its lifecycle, a database transaction progresses through several distinct execution states to guarantee ACID properties and system consistency: Active: The initial execution state where the transaction begins and executes its read and write database operations. Partially Committed: Entered immediately after the final statement has executed, but updates still reside in memory buffers and have not yet been flushed to stable disk storage. Failed: Entered when normal execution cannot proceed due to hardware failures, logical errors, or concurrency violations. Aborted: The transaction is rolled back, all dirty updates are undone, and the database is restored to its pre-transaction state. The transaction can either restart or terminate. Committed: Entered when all log records and updates are permanently recorded on stable storage, guaranteeing durability.
subject: dbms

title: Explain consistent and inconsistent states of a database using the example of a money transfer between two bank accounts that fails midway.
chunks: A consistent state satisfies all integrity constraints and business rules, while an inconsistent state violates these rules due to partial execution or unhandled failures. Bank Transfer Scenario: Consider transferring ₹1,000 from Account $A$ (initial balance ₹5,000) to Account $B$ (initial balance ₹3,000). The database consistency invariant requires that total balance $A + B = ₹8,000$. Midway Failure: The transaction executes A = A - 1000 ($A$ becomes ₹4,000). Before B = B + 1000 can execute, the system crashes. Inconsistent State: If left unrecovered, $A + B = ₹4,000 + ₹3,000 = ₹7,000$. ₹1,000 has vanished, creating an inconsistent state. Recovery to Consistent State: The recovery manager rolls back $A$ to ₹5,000 via transaction undo logs, re-establishing the invariant $A + B = ₹8,000$.
subject: dbms

title: List the different types of failures in a database system and explain how recovery from a transaction failure is carried out.
chunks: Database systems are subject to three fundamental classes of failures: Transaction Failure: Internal logical errors (e.g., divide by zero, bad input) or system errors (e.g., deadlock abort, buffer overflow). System Crash: Hardware malfunctions or operating system crashes causing volatile main memory contents to be lost without corrupting non-volatile disk storage. Disk Failure: Head crashes or bad disk sectors destroying physical storage blocks. Recovery from Transaction Failure: When a transaction fails, the recovery manager performs an UNDO operation using the transaction log. It scans the log backwards, extracts the old values (before-images) of all modified data items, writes these original values back to the database, and appends an <abort T> log record.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the lost update and dirty read problems that arise when transactions execute concurrently, with an example of each.
chunks: Concurrency anomalies occur when transactions interleave without adequate synchronization: Lost Update (Write-Write Conflict): Occurs when two transactions read the same data item and subsequently update it based on the earlier read value. The second write overwrites and obliterates the first write without incorporating its modifications. Example: Account balance is ₹100. $T_1$ reads 100 and computes 150. Concurrently, $T_2$ reads 100 and computes 120. $T_1$ writes 150, then $T_2$ writes 120. $T_1$'s ₹50 deposit is completely lost. Dirty Read (Read-Write Conflict): Occurs when transaction $T_2$ reads a data item modified by transaction $T_1$ that has not yet committed. If $T_1$ subsequently aborts, $T_2$ has acted on transient, invalid data. Example: $T_1$ updates balance from ₹100 to ₹500. $T_2$ reads ₹500 and approves a purchase. $T_1$ aborts and rolls back to ₹100. $T_2$'s read was 'dirty'.
subject: dbms

title: Distinguish between conflict serializability and view serializability with an example.
chunks: Serializability guarantees that concurrent schedules produce results identical to some serial execution: Conflict Serializability: A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting concurrent operations. This holds if and only if its precedence (conflict) graph is acyclic. Tested efficiently in polynomial time $O(V + E)$. View Serializability: A weaker, broader condition requiring identical initial reads, dependent reads, and final writes as some serial schedule. Testing view serializability is NP-complete. Example: Consider schedule $S: R_1(A), W_2(A), W_1(A), W_3(A)$. Here, operations conflict in both directions ($T_1 \to T_2$ and $T_2 \to T_1$), producing a cycle in the precedence graph; thus $S$ is not conflict serializable . However, due to blind writes ($W_3(A)$ overwriting $A$), $S$ produces the exact same view as serial schedule $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3$, making it view serializable .
subject: dbms

title: Explain the role of the concurrency control manager and the lock manager, and describe how the lock table is used to grant or queue lock requests.
chunks: The concurrency control manager ensures serializability, isolation, and consistency across interleaved transactions. It delegates resource locking to the lock manager . The lock manager maintains an in-memory hash table called the lock table , indexed by data item ID: Granted List: Holds records of transactions currently granted a lock on the item, along with lock mode (Shared $S$ or Exclusive $X$). Wait Queue: When a transaction requests an incompatible lock (e.g., $X$-lock while an $S$-lock is held), the request cannot be granted. The lock manager suspends the transaction and appends it to the item's FIFO wait queue. Release & Grant: When a lock holder unlocks the item, the lock manager inspects the wait queue, awakens compatible waiting transactions, and updates the granted list.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the role of TCL commands in controlling transactions.
chunks: Transaction Control Language (TCL) commands manage database transactions to ensure data integrity and ACID properties: COMMIT: Permanently saves all changes made by the transaction to disk. Locks are released, and modifications become visible to other concurrent users. ROLLBACK: Reverts all modifications made by an uncommitted transaction, returning the database to the state prior to transaction initiation or to a specified savepoint. SAVEPOINT: Establishes intermediate checkpoints within a transaction. Allows partial rollback (e.g., ROLLBACK TO sp1 ) without undoing the entire transaction. SET TRANSACTION: Configures isolation levels (e.g., READ COMMITTED , SERIALIZABLE ) and access modes ( READ ONLY vs READ WRITE ) before operations begin.
subject: dbms

title: With an example, explain the ACID properties of a transaction.
chunks: ACID properties guarantee reliable database transactions. Consider transferring ₹1,000 from account $A$ to account $B$: Atomicity: All operations succeed or none do. Either both debiting $A$ and crediting $B$ succeed, or the transaction aborts and leaves both balances unchanged. Consistency: The transaction transforms the database from one valid state to another, preserving integrity invariants (e.g., total funds $A + B$ remains constant before and after). Isolation: Intermediate states are hidden from concurrent transactions. Another transaction reading $A$ and $B$ cannot see $A$ deducted before $B$ is credited. Durability: Once committed, updates persist permanently on non-volatile storage, even if a power failure or system crash occurs immediately afterward.
subject: dbms

title: Consider the schedule S: R1(A), W1(A), R2(A), W2(A), R1(B), W1(B), R2(B), W2(B), where Ri and Wi denote the read and write operations of transaction Ti. Draw the precedence graph of S, determine whether S is conflict serializable and, if so, give an equivalent serial schedule.
chunks: To analyze schedule $S$, we identify all pairs of conflicting operations (operations by different transactions on the same data item where at least one is a write): Conflicts on Data Item A: $R_1(A) < W_2(A)$, $W_1(A) < R_2(A)$, and $W_1(A) < W_2(A)$ all establish precedence edge $T_1 \to T_2$. Conflicts on Data Item B: $R_1(B) < W_2(B)$, $W_1(B) < R_2(B)$, and $W_1(B) < W_2(B)$ also establish edge $T_1 \to T_2$. Graph Analysis: In a precedence graph, a directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ executes a conflicting operation before $T_j$. Here, all conflicting pairs direct from $T_1$ to $T_2$ with zero reverse edges. Serializability: Because the precedence graph contains no directed cycles (strictly acyclic), schedule $S$ is conflict serializable . Equivalent Serial Schedule: Topological ordering gives $\langle T_1, T_2 \rangle$ ($T_1$ followed by $T_2$).
subject: dbms

title: Explain log-based recovery with the deferred database modification and immediate database modification techniques.
chunks: Log-based recovery uses a write-ahead log (WAL) on stable storage to restore database consistency after crashes: Deferred Database Modification: All write operations update only the log buffer in memory; the actual database on disk is modified only after the transaction commits. Recovery Policy: Since uncommitted updates are never written to disk, an UNDO is never required (NO-UNDO/REDO algorithm). During crash recovery, the DBMS only REDOes transactions whose log contains both <T start> and <T commit> . Immediate Database Modification: Database updates can be written to disk while the transaction is still active, before committing (following WAL rules). Recovery Policy: Requires both UNDO and REDO (UNDO/REDO algorithm). Uncommitted transactions that modified disk blocks must be UNDONE, while committed transactions must be REDONE to guarantee durability.
subject: dbms

title: Explain dense and sparse indexes with an example. Which of the two requires less storage space and why?
chunks: Indexes accelerate search key lookups by mapping keys to disk block locations: Dense Index: An index record appears for every search-key value in the data file. For duplicate keys, it points to the first record or a list of records. Fast lookups, but large index footprint. Example: An employee table with 10,000 records has 10,000 entries in its dense index. Sparse Index: An index record appears for only some search-key values (typically one anchor key per disk block). Requires data records to be physically sorted by search key. Example: 10,000 records stored across 100 blocks require only 100 entries in a sparse index. Storage Comparison: A sparse index requires significantly less storage space because it contains far fewer entries, allowing it to remain memory-resident and reducing I/O operations.
subject: dbms

title: Explain the unrepeatable read and phantom read problems of concurrent transactions with an example for each.
chunks: These two read anomalies occur under relaxed SQL isolation levels: Unrepeatable (Fuzzy) Read: Transaction $T_1$ reads a specific row. Concurrently, transaction $T_2$ modifies or deletes that row and commits. When $T_1$ re-reads the exact same row, it discovers that the values have changed or the row disappeared. Example: $T_1$ reads employee John's salary as ₹50,000. $T_2$ updates John's salary to ₹60,000 and commits. $T_1$ re-reads John's record and finds ₹60,000, violating read repeatability. Phantom Read: Transaction $T_1$ reads a set of rows satisfying a search predicate. Concurrently, transaction $T_2$ inserts a new row matching that predicate and commits. When $T_1$ re-executes the query, a new 'phantom' row appears. Example: $T_1$ runs SELECT count(*) WHERE dept='IT' (gets 5). $T_2$ inserts a new IT employee and commits. $T_1$ re-runs the count and gets 6.
subject: dbms

title: Distinguish between serial and non-serial schedules. Define conflict serializability and explain why a DBMS needs serializable schedules.
chunks: A schedule defines the chronological execution sequence of operations across concurrent transactions. 1. Serial vs. Non-Serial Schedules: Feature Serial Schedule Non-Serial (Interleaved) Schedule Execution Order Operations of each transaction execute consecutively without interleaving. Operations of multiple transactions interleave concurrently. Throughput & CPU Poor CPU and I/O resource utilization; waiting transactions block everything. High throughput and optimal resource utilization during I/O stalls. Consistency Always preserves consistency automatically without concurrency control. Can lead to anomalies (lost updates, dirty reads) unless serialized. Response Time High turnaround time for long transactions. Significantly reduced latency for short transactions. 2. Conflict Serializability: A non-serial schedule $S$ is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into an equivalent serial schedule by a sequence of swaps of non-conflicting adjacent operations. Two operations conflict if they are issued by different transactions, operate on the same data item, and at least one is a write operation ($R_i(X)-W_j(X)$, $W_i(X)-R_j(X)$, or $W_i(X)-W_j(X)$). A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph (conflict graph) contains no directed cycles. 3. Why a DBMS Needs Serializable Schedules: Guaranteed Correctness: Since any serial execution preserves database consistency, a serializable concurrent schedule guarantees that the final state is mathematically correct. Concurrency without Inconsistency: Allows the DBMS to maximize hardware parallelism, multi-core CPU throughput, and disk I/O overlap while completely eliminating race conditions and isolation anomalies. ACID Isolation Invariant: Commercial database engines mandate serializability to fulfill the SQL standard Isolation requirement without forcing transactions to run strictly one at a time.
subject: dbms

title: Explain recoverable, non-recoverable and cascadeless schedules and cascading rollback, giving a short example schedule for each.
chunks: Transaction recovery properties define how concurrent schedules behave when uncommitted dependencies encounter unexpected failures or aborts: 1. Non-Recoverable Schedule: Occurs when transaction $T_2$ reads a data item modified by uncommitted transaction $T_1$, and $T_2$ commits before $T_1$. If $T_1$ subsequently aborts, $T_2$ has committed dirty data that cannot be rolled back without violating the Durability property of ACID. Example: $S_1: W_1(A), R_2(A), Commit(T_2), Abort(T_1)$. Once $T_2$ commits, its results are permanently written to disk, leaving the database in an unrecoverable corrupted state. 2. Recoverable Schedule: A schedule is recoverable if, whenever transaction $T_2$ reads a data item written by transaction $T_1$, the commit operation of $T_1$ precedes the commit operation of $T_2$ ($Commit(T_1) < Commit(T_2)$). Example: $S_2: W_1(A), R_2(A), Commit(T_1), Commit(T_2)$. If $T_1$ aborts instead, $T_2$ has not yet committed and can be safely aborted too. 3. Cascading Rollback: A phenomenon where the failure and rollback of a single transaction triggers a chain reaction of aborts across multiple dependent, uncommitted transactions that read its dirty uncommitted updates. Example: $S_3: W_1(A), R_2(A), W_2(B), R_3(B), Abort(T_1)$. Because $T_1$ aborts, $T_2$ must abort, which in turn forces $T_3$ to abort, squandering significant CPU and disk I/O work. 4. Cascadeless Schedule: A schedule is

cascadeless (avoids cascading aborts) if every transaction reads only values written by already committed transactions ($Read_j(X)$ is delayed until after $Commit(T_i)$). Example: $S_4: W_1(A), Commit(T_1), R_2(A), Commit(T_2)$. Since $T_2$ only reads after $T_1$ commits, an abort of $T_1$ can never affect $T_2$. Every cascadeless schedule is strictly recoverable. Containment Hierarchy: The classes of schedules satisfy the strict inclusion relation: $\text{Strict Schedules} \subset \text{Cascadeless Schedules} \subset \text{Recoverable Schedules} \subset \text{All Possible Schedules}$. Commercial database engines enforce cascadelessness or strictness to maintain continuous system throughput.
subject: dbms

title: Explain how deadlocks are detected using a wait-for graph, and explain the deadlock recovery schemes: victim selection, rollback and the avoidance of starvation.
chunks: A deadlock occurs in lock-based concurrency control when transactions enter circular wait states for held locks. 1. Deadlock Detection via Wait-For Graph (WFG): A Wait-For Graph is a directed graph $G = (V, E)$ maintained dynamically by the lock manager where vertices $V$ represent active transactions and directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ is suspended waiting for a lock currently held by $T_j$. When a lock request cannot be granted, an edge is added; when a lock is released, corresponding edges are deleted. The lock manager invokes cycle-detection algorithms (e.g., Depth-First Search or Tarjan's strongly connected components algorithm) at scheduled intervals. A deadlock exists if and only if the WFG contains a directed cycle. 2. Deadlock Recovery Schemes: Victim Selection: When a cycle is detected, the DBMS chooses one transaction in the cycle to abort. The selection minimizes overall rollback overhead based on criteria such as elapsed execution time, remaining queries, number of modified rows, and number of cascading rollbacks prevented. Rollback Policy: Total Rollback: Abort the victim completely and restart it from the very beginning. Partial Rollback: Roll back the victim only to an intermediate savepoint sufficient to release the contested lock and break the graph cycle,

saving prior computational work. Avoidance of Starvation: If victim selection always chooses the youngest transaction or the one with the fewest updates, that transaction could repeatedly be aborted and starved from ever finishing. To prevent starvation, the DBMS associates an abort count with each transaction; each abort increments its priority so an older transaction is never starved indefinitely.
subject: dbms

title: Explain shared (S) and exclusive (X) locks along with the lock compatibility matrix, and describe the basic two-phase locking protocol, including its growing phase, shrinking phase and lock point.
chunks: Lock-based concurrency control protocols restrict concurrent data access using complementary lock modes and acquisition phases: 1. Shared (S) and Exclusive (X) Locks: Shared Lock ($S$): Read-only lock mode. If a transaction holds a shared lock on data item $Q$, other concurrent transactions can also acquire shared locks on $Q$ ($S-S$ is compatible). No writes are permitted. Exclusive Lock ($X$): Read-write lock mode. Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock on $Q$ at any given moment ($X-S$ and $X-X$ are strictly incompatible). Lock Compatibility Matrix: Requested \ Held Shared ($S$) Exclusive ($X$) Shared ($S$) Compatible (True) Incompatible (False) Exclusive ($X$) Incompatible (False) Incompatible (False) 2. Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol: The basic 2PL protocol guarantees conflict serializability by requiring every transaction to separate its lock operations into two distinct, non-overlapping phases: Phase 1: Growing (Expanding) Phase: The transaction acquires new locks as needed and may upgrade locks ($S \to X$). It cannot release any lock under any circumstances. Lock Point: The exact instant when the transaction acquires its final lock (reaches peak lock count). The chronological order of lock points across transactions dictates their exact conflict serialization order. Phase 2: Shrinking (Contracting) Phase: The transaction releases held locks and may downgrade locks ($X \to S$). It cannot acquire any new locks once this phase begins. Serializability Guarantee: Because transactions never acquire new locks after releasing an earlier lock, no circular data item dependencies can be created, proving that 2PL guarantees conflict serializability.
subject: dbms

title: Compare strict and rigorous two-phase locking with the help of an example, and state the benefits of each.
chunks: Strict 2PL and Rigorous 2PL are specialized variants of the Two-Phase Locking protocol that enforce stronger guarantees than basic 2PL. 1. Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL): Rule: In addition to basic 2PL rules, a transaction must hold all its exclusive ($X$) locks until it terminates (commits or aborts). Shared ($S$) locks can be released during the shrinking phase before commit. Benefits: Guarantees recoverable and cascadeless schedules (prevents dirty reads), simplifying transaction rollback without cascading aborts. Allows concurrent reads to proceed earlier when shared locks are released. 2. Rigorous Two-Phase Locking (Rigorous 2PL): Rule: A transaction must hold all locks (both Shared $S$ and Exclusive $X$) until it terminates (commits or aborts). The shrinking phase collapses to the commit/abort point. Benefits: Guarantees strict serializability. Transactions can be serialized in the exact order in which they commit, making schedule analysis and replication coordination straightforward. 3. Comparative Example Schedule: Consider transaction $T_1$ needing to read $A$ and update $B$, and transaction $T_2$ needing to read $A$: Under Strict 2PL: $T_1$ acquires $S(A)$ and $X(B)$. After reading $A$, $T_1$ can release $S(A)$ early. $T_2$ can immediately acquire $S(A)$ and read $A$ before $T_1$ commits. However, $T_1$ retains $X(B)$ until commit. Under Rigorous 2PL: $T_1$

acquires $S(A)$ and $X(B)$. $T_1$ cannot release $S(A)$ until it commits. $T_2$ must wait if it needs an exclusive lock, ensuring strict chronological locking isolation. Dimension Strict 2PL Rigorous 2PL X-locks held until Commit / Abort Commit / Abort S-locks held until Can release in shrinking phase Commit / Abort Concurrency Level Higher (early S-lock release) Lower (locks held longer) Commit Ordering May differ from lock point Identical to commit order
subject: dbms

title: Explain the architecture of a data warehouse (data sources, staging area, warehouse and presentation layer), describe the ETL process and state the role of data marts.
chunks: A Data Warehouse (DW) is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, and non-volatile collection of corporate data structured for management decision-support analysis. 1. Architectural Layers: Data Sources: Operational transactional databases (OLTP), enterprise ERP and CRM systems, flat log files, web clickstreams, and third-party APIs. Staging Area: An intermediate holding and processing area where incoming data is extracted, sanitized, validated, and normalized before warehouse insertion, isolating production OLTP systems from query load. Warehouse (Enterprise Storage): The central repository storing integrated historical and atomic granular data organized according to enterprise-wide relational or dimensional data models. Presentation Layer: Front-end client applications providing reporting dashboards, OLAP multidimensional cubes, data visualization, and predictive data mining tools. Metadata Repository: Maintains administrative schemas, ETL business rules, transformation lineage, and indexing definitions, serving as the system directory across all warehouse components. 2. The ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) Process: Extract: Captures changed data (CDC) from heterogeneous relational databases, legacy systems, and unstructured files without interrupting live transaction processing. Transform: Performs critical data cleansing (handling null values and duplicates), standardizing disparate formats (e.g., converting dates to ISO standard, harmonizing currency codes), joining reference data, and generating artificial surrogate primary keys. Load: Executes bulk insertions of curated records into the target warehouse fact

and dimension tables during scheduled batch loading windows. 3. Role of Data Marts: A data mart is a departmental, highly focused subset of the warehouse customized for specific business units (such as Marketing, Finance, or Logistics). By structuring data into dedicated star or snowflake schemas, data marts deliver accelerated query performance, tighter security isolation, and tailored analytics without traversing the massive enterprise warehouse.
subject: dbms

title: Why is two-phase locking (mostly strict 2PL) used in commercial DBMSs? Show with an example schedule that it can still cause deadlock, and write its other drawbacks.
chunks: Commercial database engines (such as Oracle, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server) overwhelmingly implement Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) as their primary concurrency control protocol. 1. Why Commercial DBMSs Adopt Strict 2PL: Guarantees Serializability: Like basic 2PL, it mathematically guarantees that all concurrent interleaved schedules are conflict serializable. Eliminates Cascading Aborts: By holding exclusive ($X$) locks until commit, transactions never write data that others read uncommitted; schedules are strictly cascadeless and recoverable. Simple Crash Recovery: Transaction rollback requires only undoing before-images without inspecting or aborting other transactions. 2. Deadlock Schedule Example under Strict 2PL: Strict 2PL does not prevent deadlocks. Consider two transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ accessing data items $A$ and $B$: $T_1$ acquires $X(A)$ and writes to $A$. $T_2$ acquires $X(B)$ and writes to $B$. $T_1$ requests $X(B)$: since $T_2$ holds $X(B)$ until commit, $T_1$ must wait for $T_2$. $T_2$ requests $X(A)$: since $T_1$ holds $X(A)$ until commit, $T_2$ must wait for $T_1$. Both transactions hold resources while waiting for each other ($T_1 \to T_2 \to T_1$), creating a mutual deadlock that requires DBMS intervention. 3. Drawbacks of Two-Phase Locking: Deadlock Overhead: Systems must dedicate CPU cycles to maintain wait-for graphs, run cycle-detection routines, and abort/restart victims. Reduced Concurrency & Lock

Convoying: Long-running write transactions holding exclusive locks stall all subsequent readers and writers, degrading multi-user throughput. Lock Maintenance Cost: Allocating, updating, and hashing lock table entries adds memory consumption and lock manager processing latency. Phantom Anomalies: Tuple-level 2PL cannot stop phantom inserts into range queries unless expensive predicate/index-range locking is used.

title: Explain the deadlock prevention schemes Wait-Die and Wound-Wait with examples.
chunks: Deadlock prevention protocols use transaction timestamps to decide whether a requesting transaction should wait or abort when a resource conflict occurs. Monotonic timestamp $TS(T_i)$ is assigned when transaction $T_i$ begins (smaller timestamp implies older transaction). Suppose transaction $T_i$ requests a lock held by transaction $T_j$: 1. Wait-Die Scheme (Non-Preemptive): Older requests from Younger ($TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ is allowed to wait . Younger requests from Older ($TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ dies (aborts) and restarts with its original timestamp. Rule Summary: 'Old waits, young dies.' Locks are never preemptively stolen. Example: Let $TS(T_1)=10$ (older) and $TS(T_2)=20$ (younger). If $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$, $T_1$ waits. If $T_2$ requests a lock held by $T_1$, $T_2$ dies and restarts. 2. Wound-Wait Scheme (Preemptive): Older requests from Younger ($TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ wounds $T_j$; $T_j$ is preempted, aborted, and rolls back, releasing its lock to $T_i$. $T_j$ restarts with its original timestamp. Younger requests from Older ($TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ is allowed to wait . Rule Summary: 'Old wounds, young waits.' Younger transactions are preempted by older ones. Example: With $TS(T_1)=10$ and $TS(T_2)=20$, if $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$, $T_1$ preempts ($T_2$ is aborted). If $T_2$ requests a lock held

by $T_1$, $T_2$ waits. 3. Key Comparison: Metric Wait-Die Wound-Wait Preemption Non-preemptive Preemptive Number of Aborts High (young transactions die repeatedly) Fewer aborts; locks granted quickly to old Starvation Avoided (retains original timestamp) Avoided (retains original timestamp) Starvation Freedom Guarantee: In both schemes, when an aborted transaction restarts, it keeps its original starting timestamp. Thus, as time passes, the transaction becomes progressively older relative to new transactions, guaranteeing that it eventually becomes the oldest active transaction and runs to completion without ever dying again.

title: Construct a B+ tree in which every node can hold at most 3 keys (a maximum of 4 child pointers) by inserting the keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70 in the given order. Show the tree after every node split and state two advantages of a B+ tree over a B-tree.
chunks: Node Specification: Max keys $M = 3$, maximum child pointers $P = 4$. A node splits when the number of keys reaches 4. Step-by-Step Construction: Insert 10, 20, 30: All fit in the single root leaf node: [10, 20, 30] . Insert 40 (Split 1): Node overflows to [10, 20, 30, 40] . In a B+ tree leaf split, the middle key (index $\lceil 4/2 \rceil = 2$, key 30) is copied up to the parent. Left leaf keeps [10, 20] , right leaf keeps [30, 40] with a leaf sibling pointer. New root becomes [30] . Insert 50: Placed into right leaf: [30, 40, 50] . Tree valid. Insert 60 (Split 2): Right leaf overflows to [30, 40, 50, 60] . Leaf splits: left leaf retains [30, 40] , right leaf gets [50, 60] , and key 50 is copied up to root. Root now contains keys [30, 50] . Insert 70: Placed into rightmost leaf: [50, 60, 70] . Node is full but does not exceed 3 keys. Two Distinct Advantages of a B+ Tree over a Standard B-Tree: Extremely Fast Sequential Range Queries: In a B+ tree, all leaf nodes are linked into a continuous linked list.

Range queries execute by jumping to the start key via root search and simply scanning linearly across leaf sibling pointers, completely avoiding expensive in-order tree traversals required by B-trees. Higher Fanout and Lower Tree Height: Internal nodes in a B+ tree store only search keys and child pointers without actual data records. Consequently, each fixed-size disk page fits significantly more branch pointers (higher fanout), making the tree shallower and drastically reducing the number of disk I/O operations required for lookups.

title: A static hash file uses the hash function h(k) = k mod 5. Each bucket holds at most 2 records and overflow is handled by chaining. Insert the keys 5, 12, 21, 9, 17, 14, 8, 33, 22 and 7 in the given order and show the final contents of each bucket. Also explain how extendible hashing avoids long overflow chains. 5 Sr. No. Question Marks 120 A retail chain wants to analyse its sales by store, product and month. (i) Design a star schema with one fact table and suitable dimension tables. (ii) Explain the OLAP operations roll -up, drill-down and slice with an example from this schema. (iii) Analyse how the OLAP workload on this warehouse differs from the OLTP workload of the stores' billing systems.
chunks: Part 1: Static Hashing ($h(k) = k \bmod 5$, Bucket Capacity = 2, Chaining): $k=5: 5 \bmod 5 = 0 \to$ Bucket 0: [5] $k=12: 12 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2: [12] $k=21: 21 \bmod 5 = 1 \to$ Bucket 1: [21] $k=9: 9 \bmod 5 = 4 \to$ Bucket 4: [9] $k=17: 17 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2: [12, 17] (Full) $k=14: 14 \bmod 5 = 4 \to$ Bucket 4: [9, 14] (Full) $k=8: 8 \bmod 5 = 3 \to$ Bucket 3: [8] $k=33: 33 \bmod 5 = 3 \to$ Bucket 3: [8, 33] (Full) $k=22: 22 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2 overflows $\to$ Chained Overflow Block: [22] $k=7: 7 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2 overflow chain: [22, 7] Final Bucket Contents: Bucket 0: [5] ; Bucket 1: [21] ; Bucket 2: Primary [12, 17] $\to$ Chained Overflow [22, 7] ; Bucket 3: [8, 33] ; Bucket 4: [9, 14] . How Extendible Hashing Avoids Long Chains: Extendible hashing uses a dynamic directory with global and local depth. When a bucket overflows, only that specific bucket splits, doubling its local depth. If local depth exceeds global depth, the directory doubles. Records

are redistributed using additional hash bits, preventing sequential linear overflow search degradation. Part 2: Retail Star Schema & OLAP Workload: Star Schema Design: Central fact table Sales_Fact with measures ( quantity_sold , total_revenue ) and foreign keys ( store_id , product_id , time_id ), surrounded by dimension tables Store_Dim (location, city), Product_Dim (category, brand), and Time_Dim (day, month, quarter, year). OLAP Operations: Roll-up: Aggregates sales from Month to Year level. Drill-down: De-aggregates sales from Product Category down to individual Item. Slice: Filters sales for a single store (e.g., store_id = 'Store_101' ). OLAP vs. OLTP Workload: Store billing (OLTP) executes frequent, short, write-intensive ACID transactions with normalized schemas. The warehouse (OLAP) executes long-running, read-mostly, complex multi-table analytical aggregations over millions of denormalized historical records.
