title: Check whether the following relations on Z are equivalence relations: (i) xRy if |x − y| is even; (ii) xRy if x2 = y2; (iii) xRy if xy ≥ 0.
chunks: An equivalence relation on $\mathbb{Z}$ must be reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. (i) $x R y \iff |x - y|$ is even: Reflexive: For any $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, $|x - x| = |0| = 0 = 2 \times 0$, which is even. Thus $x R x$. Symmetric: If $x R y$, then $|x - y| = 2k$ for some $k \ge 0$. Since $|y - x| = |-(x - y)| = |x - y| = 2k$, $|y - x|$ is even, so $y R x$. Transitive: $|x - y|$ is even $\iff x - y$ is even. If $x - y = 2k_1$ and $y - z = 2k_2$, then $(x - y) + (y - z) = x - z = 2(k_1 + k_2)$. Since $k_1 + k_2 \in \mathbb{Z}$, $x - z$ is even $\implies |x - z|$ is even, so $x R z$. Conclusion: Yes, it is an equivalence relation (partitions $\mathbb{Z}$ into Even and Odd integers). (ii) $x R y \iff x^2 = y^2$: Reflexive: For all $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, $x^2 = x^2$ holds identically. Thus $x R x$. Symmetric: If $x^2 = y^2$, then $y^2 = x^2$ by symmetry of equality. Thus $y R x$. Transitive:

If $x^2 = y^2$ and $y^2 = z^2$, then $x^2 = z^2$ by transitivity of equality. Thus $x R z$. Conclusion: Yes, it is an equivalence relation (equivalence classes are $\{0\}$ and pairs $\{x, -x\}$ for $x \ne 0$). (iii) $x R y \iff x y \ge 0$: Reflexive: For all $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, $x \cdot x = x^2 \ge 0$ holds. Thus $x R x$. Symmetric: If $x y \ge 0$, then $y x = x y \ge 0$, so $y R x$. Transitive (FAILS): We provide a counterexample involving zero: Take $x = -3, y = 0, z = 4$. $x y = (-3)(0) = 0 \ge 0 \implies -3 R 0$ (holds). $y z = (0)(4) = 0 \ge 0 \implies 0 R 4$ (holds). However, $x z = (-3)(4) = -12 < 0$, so $-3 R 4$ is false . Conclusion: Because transitivity fails, it is NOT an equivalence relation .

title: Check whether the following relations on Z are reﬂexive, symmetric, anti-symmetric and transitive: (i) xRy if |x − y| is even; (ii) xRy if x ≥ y; (iii) xRy if xy < 0.

Thus $x R y \implies y R x$. Anti-symmetric: Fails. Taking $x = 1$ and $y = 3$, $|1 - 3| = 2$ is even ($1 R 3$) and $|3 - 1| = 2$ is even ($3 R 1$), but $1 \ne 3$. Transitive: Holds. If $x - y = 2k_1$ and $y - z = 2k_2$, then $x - z = 2(k_1 + k_2)$, so $|x - z|$ is even. Thus $x R y \land y R z \implies x R z$. Taking $x = 5, y = 2$, $5 \ge 2$ ($5 R 2$), but $2 \ge 5$ is false ($2 \cancel{R} 5$). Anti-symmetric:

Holds. If $x \ge y$ and $y \ge x$, standard order arithmetic yields $x = y$. Transitive: Holds. If $x \ge y$ and $y \ge z$, transitivity of inequalities guarantees $x \ge z$. (iii) Relation $x R y \iff xy < 0$: Reflexive: Fails. For any $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, $x^2 \ge 0$, which is never strictly negative ($< 0$). Thus $x \cancel{R} x$. Symmetric: Holds. Multiplication is commutative: $x y < 0 \implies y x < 0$. Thus $x R y \implies y R x$. Anti-symmetric: Fails. For $x = 2, y = -1$: $2(-1) = -2 < 0$ ($2 R -1$) and $(-1)(2) = -2 < 0$ ($-1 R 2$), but $2 \ne -1$. Transitive: Fails. title: Prove that the following posets are lattices: (i) (N, D); (ii) (S24, D).
chunks: Definition of a Lattice: A poset $(L, \le)$ is a lattice if and only if every pair of elements $a, b \in L$ has a unique greatest lower bound (meet: $a \wedge b$) and least upper bound (join: $a \vee b$). (i) Proof that $(\mathbb{N}, D)$ is a lattice: Let $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$ with divisibility relation $D$ ($a \le b \iff a \mid b$). For any $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$: Meet ($a \wedge b = \gcd(a, b)$): By the Euclidean algorithm, the greatest common divisor $g = \gcd(a, b)$ exists in $\mathbb{N}$. It satisfies $g \mid a$ and $g \mid b$ (lower bound). Furthermore, if $c \mid a$ and $c \mid b$, then by Bézout's identity $c \mid g$ (greatest lower bound). Hence $\text{glb}(a, b) = \gcd(a, b)$ is unique. Join ($a \vee b = \text{lcm}(a, b)$): The least common multiple $m = \text{lcm}(a, b) = \frac{ab}{\gcd(a, b)}$ exists in $\mathbb{N}$. It satisfies $a \mid m$ and $b \mid m$ (upper bound). If $a \mid k$ and $b \mid k$, then $m \mid k$ (least upper bound). Hence $\text{lub}(a, b) = \text{lcm}(a, b)$ is unique. Since both glb and lub exist uniquely for every pair, $(\mathbb{N}, D)$

is a lattice . (ii) Proof that $(S_{24}, D)$ is a lattice: The set $S_{24} = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24\}$ consists of all positive divisors of 24. We demonstrate closure under the lattice operations: Closure under meet ($\gcd$): If $a, b \in S_{24}$, then $a \mid 24$. Since $\gcd(a, b) \mid a$, by transitivity $\gcd(a, b) \mid 24$. Hence $\gcd(a, b) \in S_{24}$. Closure under join ($\text{lcm}$): Since $a \mid 24$ and $b \mid 24$, 24 is a common multiple of $a$ and $b$. By definition of least common multiple, $\text{lcm}(a, b) \mid 24$. Hence $\text{lcm}(a, b) \in S_{24}$. Since $S_{24}$ is closed under $\gcd$ and $\text{lcm}$, every pair in $S_{24}$ has its glb and lub in $S_{24}$. Therefore, $(S_{24}, D)$ is a lattice .
