title: A process has Base Register = 1000 and Limit Register = 300. Calculate the physical address for logical address 250, and state whether logical address 350 would be allowed.
chunks: The MMU validates logical addresses using the condition $\text{Logical Address} < \text{Limit Register}$. When valid, $\text{Physical Address} = \text{Base Register} + \text{Logical Address}$. For Logical Address 250: Validation: $250 < 300$ is True (address is valid). Physical Address Calculation: $$\text{Physical Address} = 1000 + 250 = \mathbf{1250}$$ For Logical Address 350: Validation: $350 < 300$ is False . Result: Access is not allowed . The hardware triggers a trap to the operating system (illegal addressing / segmentation fault), aborting the illegal memory access.
subject: os

title: A partition of size 100 KB is allocated to a process of size 70 KB. Identify the type of fragmentation that occurs here and state the amount of wasted memory.
chunks: Evaluation of Memory Allocation: Type of Fragmentation: Internal Fragmentation . It occurs because a fixed partition allocated to a process is larger than the process's actual memory requirement, leaving unused memory reserved within that partition. Amount of Wasted Memory: $$\text{Internal Fragmentation} = \text{Partition Size} - \text{Process Size} = 100\text{ KB} - 70\text{ KB} = \mathbf{30\text{ KB}}$$ This 30 KB remains locked inside the partition and cannot be allocated to any other process until the current process terminates.
subject: os

title: In a Resource Allocation Graph with multiple-instance resources, a cycle is present but the system is not in deadlock. Explain why this can happen.
chunks: In a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG) with multiple-instance resources , a cycle is a necessary condition for deadlock, but not a sufficient condition . Cause: A resource type participating in the cycle may possess instances allocated to processes that are external to the cycle. Resolution Mechanism: When an external process completes its execution, it releases its allocated instances back to the available pool. Those freed instances can be allocated to one of the waiting processes in the cycle, satisfying its request, breaking the cyclic dependency, and averting deadlock.
subject: os

title: List the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur.
chunks: For a deadlock to arise, all four Coffman conditions must hold simultaneously within the system: Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode; only one process can use the resource at any given time. Hold and Wait: A process must currently hold at least one resource while concurrently waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly seized from a process; a resource can only be released voluntarily by the holding process upon task completion. Circular Wait: A closed chain of processes $\{P_0, P_1, \dots, P_n\}$ must exist such that $P_0$ waits for a resource held by $P_1$, $P_1$ waits for a resource held by $P_2$, ..., and $P_n$ waits for a resource held by $P_0$.
subject: os

title: Explain the difference between Deadlock Prevention and Deadlock Avoidance.
chunks: Dimension Deadlock Prevention Deadlock Avoidance Core Principle Constrains resource requests by structurally invalidating at least one of the four Coffman conditions before runtime. Allows dynamic requests, but ensures the system never enters an unsafe state by evaluating future states. Prior Information Requires no advance knowledge of future resource demands or process execution patterns. Requires a priori knowledge of the maximum resources each process will ever claim. Resource Utilization Low; imposes restrictive static rules that cause resource underutilization and potential starvation. Higher; dynamic allocation allows more concurrency, though constrained by safe-state checks. Runtime Overhead Low runtime computation overhead; enforced via structural request protocols. High runtime overhead; algorithms like the Banker's Algorithm must execute on every request.
subject: os

title: Explain the three components used in address translation: Base Register, Limit Register, and MMU.
chunks: Address translation provides process isolation and memory protection using three integrated hardware components: Base Register (Relocation Register): Stores the starting physical RAM address where the process's allocated partition begins. During execution, the base value is added to every generated logical address ($\text{Physical Address} = \text{Base} + \text{Logical}$). Limit Register: Defines the maximum valid range (size) of the process's logical address space. The CPU validates whether $\text{Logical Address} < \text{Limit}$; if the address exceeds or equals this limit, a fatal memory protection trap is triggered. Memory Management Unit (MMU): The hardware device integrated into the CPU that coordinates real-time translation and validation. The MMU intercepts logical addresses, performs the limit comparison, applies the base offset, and sends the verified physical address to the memory bus.
subject: os

title: Differentiate between Fixed (Static) Partitioning and Variable (Dynamic) Partitioning.
chunks: Feature Fixed (Static) Partitioning Variable (Dynamic) Partitioning Partition Sizing RAM is divided into predetermined, static partitions at system configuration or boot time. Partitions are created dynamically with sizes precisely tailored to each arriving process. Degree of Multiprogramming Fixed; capped strictly by the predetermined number of partitions ($N$). Dynamic; limited only by available total RAM and system descriptor overhead. Internal Fragmentation Present and severe: When a process does not fill its designated partition, leftover space is wasted. Absent: Partitions are allocated to exact requested sizes. External Fragmentation Absent: Partition boundaries never shift or fragment. Present: Process terminations leave scattered free memory holes across RAM. Process Size Constraint Processes larger than the largest single partition cannot be loaded. Any process smaller than total contiguous free memory can be loaded.
subject: os

title: Compare First Fit, Best Fit, and Worst Fit memory allocation strategies.
chunks: Strategy Search Strategy Execution Speed Memory Fragmentation Impact First Fit Scans the free hole list from the start and allocates the first hole large enough ($\text{Hole Size} \ge \text{Process Size}$). Fastest; search stops immediately upon finding the first valid block. Leaves smaller residual holes near the start of memory; exhibits strong overall storage utilization. Best Fit Scans the entire list of holes and selects the smallest hole that is large enough. Slow; must examine all holes unless maintained as a size-sorted list. Generates the smallest leftover residual holes, which often become unusable slivers (severe external fragmentation). Worst Fit Scans the entire list of holes and selects the largest available hole. Slow; must search the full list unless kept sorted in descending size. Leaves behind the largest remaining hole, which is more likely to be large enough to host another process.
subject: os

title: Explain why a cycle in a Resource Allocation Graph is a sufficient condition for deadlock with single-instance resources, but only a necessary condition with multiple-instance resources.
chunks: The significance of a cycle in a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG) depends on resource instance multiplicity: Single-Instance Resources (Necessary & Sufficient): When every resource has only one instance, an edge $R_j \to P_i$ means $P_i$ exclusively possesses the only copy of $R_j$. If a cycle exists ($P_1 \to R_1 \to P_2 \to R_2 \to P_1$), each process in the cycle is waiting for a resource held by another process in the exact same cycle. Because no other processes hold copies of these resources, no process can ever make progress. Thus, a cycle guarantees deadlock . Multiple-Instance Resources (Necessary, but NOT Sufficient): A cycle indicates circular dependency among the processes in the cycle. However, because each resource contains multiple instances, instances of the contested resource type may also be held by external processes $P_k$ outside the cycle. When $P_k$ completes, it releases its instance, which is then allocated to a waiting process in the cycle, successfully breaking the cycle and averting deadlock.
subject: os

title: Holes of size 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, and 300 KB are available. A process of 180 KB arrives. Identify which hole would be selected under First Fit, Best Fit, and Worst Fit respectively.
chunks: Given hole list in sequence: [100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB] . Arriving process size = 180 KB . First Fit: Inspects holes sequentially from the start: 100 KB: $100 < 180$ (Insufficient). 500 KB: $500 \ge 180$ (Sufficient). Selected Hole: 500 KB (Leftover fragment = $500 - 180 = \mathbf{320\text{ KB}}$). Best Fit: Identifies all qualifying holes: 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB. Calculates leftover fragments: $\min(500-180, 200-180, 300-180) = \min(320, 20, 120) = 20\text{ KB}$. Selected Hole: 200 KB (Leftover fragment = $200 - 180 = \mathbf{20\text{ KB}}$). Worst Fit: Selects the largest available hole in the entire list: $\max(100, 500, 200, 300) = 500\text{ KB}$. Selected Hole: 500 KB (Leftover fragment = $500 - 180 = \mathbf{320\text{ KB}}$).
subject: os

title: A system prevents Circular Wait by numbering resources R1(1), R2(2), R3(3) and requiring requests in increasing order. Explain whether a process requesting R3 followed by R1 would be allowed, and why.
chunks: Verdict: The request for $R_1$ will be DENIED (Not Allowed) . Justification and Protocol Analysis: Resource Ordering Protocol (Havender's Method): Assigns a unique integer $F(R)$ to each resource type: $F(R_1) = 1$, $F(R_2) = 2$, $F(R_3) = 3$. The protocol mandates that a process holding resource $R_i$ may only request $R_j$ if $F(R_j) > F(R_i)$. Evaluation: The process has already been allocated $R_3$ with $F(R_3) = 3$. It subsequently requests $R_1$ with $F(R_1) = 1$. Because $1 < 3$, this request strictly violates the monotonic increasing ordering rule. Required Protocol Action: To acquire $R_1$, the process must first release its hold on $R_3$, request $R_1$, and then re-request $R_3$ in legitimate ascending order ($R_1 \to R_3$). This guarantees that no cyclic dependency graph can ever form.
subject: os

title: A process has a memory requirement of 250 KB, but the largest available partition is 200 KB under Fixed Partitioning. Explain what happens to this process, and suggest which memory allocation technique would solve this problem.
chunks: Impact on the Process: Under Fixed (Static) Partitioning , a process must be loaded entirely into a single contiguous partition. Because the process requires 250 KB and the maximum partition size configured in the system is only 200 KB, the process cannot be accommodated . The OS rejects the process or places it into an indefinite wait state, regardless of whether total aggregate free memory across other partitions exceeds 250 KB. Recommended Solutions: Paging (Non-contiguous Allocation): Splits the process into fixed-size pages (e.g., 4 KB) and maps them into any available non-contiguous physical memory frames via a page table, eliminating the need for large contiguous memory slots. Dynamic Partitioning with Compaction: Adjusts partition sizes to exactly match process needs, combining dispersed free blocks via compaction. Virtual Memory (Demand Paging): Allows the process to execute by keeping only active portions (working set) in physical memory while retaining the rest on backing disk storage.
subject: os

title: Explain the Ostrich Algorithm for deadlock handling, and justify why operating systems like Windows and Linux still use it despite its disadvantages.
chunks: The Ostrich Algorithm: The Ostrich Algorithm is a pragmatic deadlock handling approach where the operating system ignores deadlocks entirely—analogous to an ostrich burying its head in the sand—under the assumption that deadlocks occur so rarely that the cost of avoiding or detecting them vastly exceeds the damage caused by their occurrence. Justification for Industry Adoption (Linux & Windows): Prohibitive Overhead: Deadlock avoidance algorithms (such as the Banker's Algorithm) incur $O(M \times N^2)$ overhead on every resource request, drastically slowing system throughput. Impractical Assumptions: Avoidance requires user processes to declare their maximum future resource claims in advance—an impossible demand for dynamic modern applications (browsers, IDEs, compilers). Cost-Effective Recovery: Since deadlocks are rare in well-designed user applications, it is far more practical to let the user or OS terminate an unresponsive process (via Task Manager, kill -9 ) or reboot than to penalize all computing operations continuously.
subject: os

title: Explain the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur, with one example each.
chunks: Deadlock can occur if and only if the following four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously in the system. If even one condition is prevented, deadlock cannot occur: Mutual Exclusion: Explanation: At least one resource must be held in a non-shareable mode, meaning only one process can hold and use the resource at any given moment. Any other process requesting that resource must wait until it is released. Example: A physical printer or a dedicated write lock on a database record. If process $P_1$ is printing a document, process $P_2$ cannot simultaneously send data to the same printer without corrupting the output. Hold and Wait: Explanation: A process must currently hold at least one allocated resource while simultaneously waiting to acquire one or more additional resources that are currently being held by other active processes. Example: Process $P_1$ opens and holds a DVD burner drive, and while holding it, requests an exclusive lock on an ISO disk image file that is currently being downloaded and held by process $P_2$. No Preemption: Explanation: Resources cannot be forcibly seized or preempted from a process while it is using them. A resource can only be released voluntarily and explicitly by the holding process after it

has finished its designated execution. Example: The OS cannot arbitrarily yank a tape drive away from a running backup process halfway through writing an archive without corrupting the data stream. Circular Wait: Explanation: A closed directed chain of processes $\{P_0, P_1, \dots, P_n\}$ exists such that $P_0$ is waiting for a resource held by $P_1$, $P_1$ is waiting for a resource held by $P_2$, and $P_n$ is waiting for a resource held by $P_0$. Example: Process $P_1$ holds Resource $R_1$ and requests $R_2$, while Process $P_2$ holds $R_2$ and requests $R_1$. Neither process can proceed, producing an intractable mutual blockage.
subject: os

title: Explain the three methods of deadlock recovery: Process Termination, Resource Preemption, and Process Rollback.
chunks: Once a deadlock has been detected by the operating system, the deadlock cycle must be broken using one of three primary recovery techniques: Process Termination: Involves terminating one or more processes to eliminate cyclic wait dependencies: Abort all deadlocked processes: The most drastic approach. Completely breaks the deadlock immediately, but discards all partial computations, resulting in high economic and computational cost. Abort one process at a time: The OS terminates one process and reruns the deadlock detection algorithm, repeating until the cycle is eliminated. Victim selection criteria include: process priority, execution time elapsed, remaining time to complete, resources held, and whether the process is interactive or batch. Resource Preemption: Involves forcibly taking away resources from some processes and allocating them to other deadlocked processes until the deadlock cycle is resolved. Three critical issues must be addressed: Selecting a Victim: Determine which process holds resources that can be preempted with minimum overall cost penalty. Rollback: Because a resource was preempted, the victim process cannot proceed normally. The OS must roll back the victim process to a safe checkpoint state and restart it from that point. Starvation: If the same process is repeatedly chosen as the lowest-cost victim, it may never complete.

The OS prevents this by incorporating the number of rollbacks into the process's priority calculation (aging). Process Rollback: The operating system periodically checkpoints the state of executing processes (register values, memory images, file locks). When deadlock is detected, the OS rolls back a selected process to its last saved checkpoint rather than killing it entirely, frees its recently acquired resources to resolve the deadlock, and reschedules it later.
subject: os

title: Explain Paging in detail, including the concepts of pages, frames, and the page table.
chunks: Paging is a non-contiguous memory management hardware scheme that permits the physical address space of a process to be non-contiguous, completely eliminating external fragmentation. Core Architectural Concepts: Pages: The logical address space of a process is divided into equal, fixed-size blocks called pages (typically $4\text{ KB} = 2^{12}$ bytes). Frames: Physical main memory (RAM) is divided into fixed-size blocks of the exact same size called frames . Page Table: A dedicated hardware/OS data structure maintained per process that maps each logical page number ($p$) to its corresponding physical frame number ($f$). Address Translation Mechanics: A logical address generated by the CPU is mathematically partitioned into two parts: Page Number ($p$): Used as an index into the page table to retrieve the base frame number ($f$). Page Offset ($d$): Defines the displacement within the page. Combined directly with the frame number to access the physical byte. $$\text{Logical Address} = (p, d) \xrightarrow{\text{Page Table Mapping}} \text{Physical Address} = (f, d) = (f \times \text{Page Size}) + d$$ Evaluation: Advantages: Completely eliminates external fragmentation; simplifies memory allocation (any free frame can be allocated to any process); supports memory protection and virtual memory. Disadvantages: Suffers from internal fragmentation on the last page of a process (averaging $\frac{1}{2}$ page per process); requires page table storage in RAM and translation overhead (mitigated by Translation Lookaside Buffers - TLBs).
subject: os

title: Compare Deadlock Prevention, Deadlock Avoidance, and Deadlock Detection & Recovery as three different strategies for handling deadlock.
chunks: Deadlock handling strategies represent fundamental engineering trade-offs between resource utilization, concurrency, and computational overhead: Dimension Deadlock Prevention Deadlock Avoidance Deadlock Detection & Recovery Basic Philosophy Structurally eliminates at least one of the 4 Coffman conditions beforehand. Inspects dynamic resource requests in real-time, only granting requests that keep the system in a safe state . Allows deadlocks to occur freely; runs periodic detection algorithms and initiates recovery. A Priori Information None required. Requires total maximum resource claims declared in advance by each process. None required. Resource Utilization Low; restrictive static allocation rules lead to poor utilization. Moderate to High; dynamically permits allocation as long as a safe sequence exists. High; resources are granted immediately upon request with no artificial restrictions. Runtime Overhead Low runtime computation; rules are enforced via static protocols. High runtime computation; algorithms like Banker's Algorithm run on every request ($O(M \times N^2)$). Periodic runtime computation; detection runs intermittently ($O(M \times N^2)$), plus recovery costs. Recovery Mechanism None needed; deadlocks are mathematically impossible. None needed; system never enters an unsafe/deadlocked state. Mandatory; involves process termination, checkpoint rollback, and resource preemption. Representative Algorithms Resource Ordering (Circular Wait), All-at-Once Allocation (Hold & Wait). Banker's Algorithm, Resource-Allocation Graph Algorithm for single instances. Wait-For Graph cycle detection, Banker's detection variant.
subject: os

title: Explain Contiguous Memory Allocation and differentiate between its Fixed Partitioning and Variable Partitioning types, including their advantages and disadvantages.
chunks: Contiguous Memory Allocation is a memory assignment model where each user program is allocated a single contiguous block of physical memory addresses. The operating system maintains partition tables and relocation registers to enforce boundary protection. Fixed (Static) Partitioning: Memory is divided into fixed, predefined partitions (equal or unequal sizes) at system initialization. Advantages: Simple to implement; low OS scheduling and management overhead. Disadvantages: Internal Fragmentation: Significant memory is wasted inside partitions when processes are smaller than partition slots. Fixed Multiprogramming: Degree of multiprogramming is capped by the number of partitions ($N$). Process Size Limit: Processes larger than the maximum partition cannot be executed. Variable (Dynamic) Partitioning: Partitions are created dynamically with sizes matching the exact memory requirements of incoming processes. Advantages: Completely eliminates internal fragmentation; supports a flexible degree of multiprogramming; processes can be as large as total physical RAM. Disadvantages: External Fragmentation: As processes terminate and leave memory, free space gets fragmented into non-contiguous holes. Compaction Overhead: Requires expensive memory shuffling (compaction) to combine fragmented holes. Search Overhead: Requires algorithms like First Fit, Best Fit, or Worst Fit to locate suitable memory holes.
subject: os

title: Compare Paging and Segmentation on the basis of division, fragmentation, and preservation of program structure.
chunks: Paging and Segmentation represent the two foundational non-contiguous memory management paradigms: Parameter Paging Segmentation Division of Memory Hardware-centric: Divides logical memory into fixed-sized pages and physical memory into identical frames (e.g., 4 KB). Division is transparent to programmer. User-centric: Divides memory into variable-sized logical blocks (segments) matching program modules (code, stack, heap, data). Fragmentation Suffers from Internal Fragmentation on the last page of a process. Absolutely immune to External Fragmentation . Suffers from External Fragmentation as variable segments are loaded/freed. Free of Internal Fragmentation . Preservation of Program Structure None: The linear address space is arbitrarily split across frame boundaries; functions or data structures may span across two physical pages. Preserved: Directly mirrors the programmer's view of modular software; each logical entity (subroutine, array) resides intact within its own segment. Address Translation 1D linear address divided by hardware into Page Number ($p$) and Offset ($d$). 2D address: Segment Number ($s$) and Offset ($d$); requires strict comparison against Segment Limit Register. Protection & Sharing Difficult to share logical units unless perfectly aligned to page boundaries. Natural and clean; entire logical segments (e.g., shared libraries) can be shared with uniform read/execute permissions.

title: Consider the following system state (Total Resources: A = 10, B = 5, C = 7):
chunks: Problem Statement: Total Resources: $A = 10, B = 5, C = 7$. Given 4 processes ($P_0, P_1, P_2, P_3$) with Allocation and Max matrices below, determine the Available resources, compute the Need matrix, and find a safe sequence using the Banker's Algorithm . Process Allocation (A, B, C) Max (A, B, C) $P_0$ 0, 1, 0 7, 5, 3 $P_1$ 2, 0, 0 3, 2, 2 $P_2$ 3, 0, 2 9, 0, 2 $P_3$ 2, 1, 1 4, 2, 2

Step 1: Calculate Total Allocated and Available Resources $\sum \text{Allocation}_A = 0 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 7$ $\sum \text{Allocation}_B = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2$ $\sum \text{Allocation}_C = 0 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 3$ $\text{Total Allocated} = (7, 2, 3)$ $$\text{Available} = \text{Total} - \text{Total Allocated} = (10, 5, 7) - (7, 2, 3) = \mathbf{(3, 3, 4)}$$

Step 2: Calculate the Need Matrix Using the formula $\text{Need}[i] = \text{Max}[i] - \text{Allocation}[i]$: Process Max Allocation Need = Max - Allocation $P_0$ (7, 5, 3) (0, 1, 0) $(7-0, 5-1, 3-0) = \mathbf{(7, 4, 3)}$ $P_1$ (3, 2, 2) (2, 0, 0) $(3-2, 2-0, 2-0) = \mathbf{(1, 2, 2)}$ $P_2$ (9, 0, 2) (3, 0, 2) $(9-3, 0-0, 2-2) = \mathbf{(6, 0, 0)}$ $P_3$ (4, 2, 2) (2, 1, 1) $(4-2, 2-1, 2-1) = \mathbf{(2, 1, 1)}$

Step 3: Safety Algorithm Execution Initialize $\text{Work} = \text{Available} = (3, 3, 4)$ and $\text{Finish}[P_i] = \text{False}$ for all $i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$. Iteration 1: Test $P_0$: $\text{Need}(7, 4, 3) \le \text{Work}(3, 3, 4) \implies$ False ($7 > 3$). Cannot execute. Test $P_1$: $\text{Need}(1, 2, 2) \le \text{Work}(3, 3, 4) \implies (1 \le 3, 2 \le 3, 2 \le 4) \implies$ True . Execute $P_1$: $$\text{New Work} = \text{Work} + \text{Allocation}(P_1) = (3, 3, 4) + (2, 0, 0) = \mathbf{(5, 3, 4)}$$ Set $\text{Finish}[P_1] = \text{True}$. Safe sequence: $\langle P_1 \rangle$. Iteration 2: With $\text{Work} = (5, 3, 4)$: Test $P_0$: $\text{Need}(7, 4, 3) \le \text{Work}(5, 3, 4) \implies$ False ($7 > 5$). Test $P_2$: $\text{Need}(6, 0, 0) \le \text{Work}(5, 3, 4) \implies$ False ($6 > 5$). Test $P_3$: $\text{Need}(2, 1, 1) \le \text{Work}(5, 3, 4) \implies (2 \le 5, 1 \le 3, 1 \le 4) \implies$ True . Execute $P_3$: $$\text{New Work} = \text{Work} + \text{Allocation}(P_3) = (5, 3, 4) + (2, 1, 1) = \mathbf{(7, 4, 5)}$$ Set $\text{Finish}[P_3] = \text{True}$. Safe sequence: $\langle P_1, P_3 \rangle$. Iteration 3: With $\text{Work} = (7, 4, 5)$: Test $P_0$: $\text{Need}(7, 4, 3) \le \text{Work}(7, 4, 5) \implies

(7 \le 7, 4 \le 4, 3 \le 5) \implies$ True . Execute $P_0$: $$\text{New Work} = \text{Work} + \text{Allocation}(P_0) = (7, 4, 5) + (0, 1, 0) = \mathbf{(7, 5, 5)}$$ Set $\text{Finish}[P_0] = \text{True}$. Safe sequence: $\langle P_1, P_3, P_0 \rangle$. Iteration 4: With $\text{Work} = (7, 5, 5)$: Test $P_2$: $\text{Need}(6, 0, 0) \le \text{Work}(7, 5, 5) \implies (6 \le 7, 0 \le 5, 0 \le 5) \implies$ True . Execute $P_2$: $$\text{New Work} = \text{Work} + \text{Allocation}(P_2) = (7, 5, 5) + (3, 0, 2) = \mathbf{(10, 5, 7)}$$ Set $\text{Finish}[P_2] = \text{True}$. Safe sequence: $\langle P_1, P_3, P_0, P_2 \rangle$.

Conclusion Since all processes have $\text{Finish}[i] = \text{True}$, the system is in a SAFE STATE . Valid Safe Sequence: $\mathbf{\langle P_1, P_3, P_0, P_2 \rangle}$ (alternatively, $\mathbf{\langle P_1, P_3, P_2, P_0 \rangle}$ is also valid).

title: A dynamic (variable) partitioning system has one large free block of 500 KB. Process A (120 KB) and Process B (180 KB) are loaded one after another, and then Process A finishes execution. Explain the resulting hole structure, why this is called external fragmentation, and how Compaction would resolve it.
chunks: Step-by-Step Scenario Analysis: Initial State: A single continuous free block of 500 KB spanning $[0, 500\text{ KB}]$. Process Allocation: Process A (120 KB) is loaded: Allocated at $[0, 120\text{ KB}]$. Remaining free memory is $[120, 500\text{ KB}]$ (380 KB). Process B (180 KB) is loaded: Allocated contiguously at $[120, 300\text{ KB}]$. Remaining free memory is $[300, 500\text{ KB}]$ (200 KB). Process A Finishes and Terminates: Process A releases its memory $[0, 120\text{ KB}]$. The resulting memory layout becomes: Hole 1: 120 KB free at addresses $[0, 120\text{ KB}]$. Process B: 180 KB allocated at addresses $[120, 300\text{ KB}]$. Hole 2: 200 KB free at addresses $[300, 500\text{ KB}]$. Why this is External Fragmentation: The total available free memory in the system is: $$\text{Total Free Memory} = 120\text{ KB} + 200\text{ KB} = \mathbf{320\text{ KB}}$$ If a new Process C arrives requiring 250 KB , the request cannot be satisfied despite 320 KB of total free space, because the free memory is non-contiguous and split into two smaller isolated holes (120 KB and 200 KB), neither of which can hold 250 KB individually. This phenomenon is precisely External Fragmentation . How Compaction Resolves It: Compaction (memory defragmentation) shifts all allocated processes

toward one end of physical memory and merges all scattered holes into a single contiguous free block: Process B is relocated downward to address $[0, 180\text{ KB}]$. Hole 1 (120 KB) and Hole 2 (200 KB) combine into one large contiguous free block of $120 + 200 = \mathbf{320\text{ KB}}$ at $[180, 500\text{ KB}]$. Process C (250 KB) can now be allocated immediately into the newly consolidated 320 KB contiguous block. Requirement: Compaction is feasible only if relocation is dynamic and supported at execution time using hardware base registers.
subject: os

title: A bank uses the Circular Wait prevention technique (resource ordering) for deadlock prevention, while an embedded medical device system that cannot afford to lose any work uses Deadlock Avoidance via the Banker's Algorithm instead. Explain why each system chose its respective strategy, considering the trade-off between flexibility and overhead.
chunks: The selection of deadlock strategies between high-throughput banking systems and safety-critical medical devices illustrates fundamental engineering trade-offs: Banking System: Deadlock Prevention via Resource Ordering System Characteristics: Millions of concurrent transactions, highly dynamic database records, stringent low-latency requirements. Why Resource Ordering: Enforcing a global canonical resource hierarchy (e.g., always locking bank accounts in strictly increasing Account ID order: $\text{lock}(\min(A, B))$ then $\text{lock}(\max(A, B))$) makes Circular Wait mathematically impossible. Trade-Off Assessment: Imposes minimal runtime overhead (simple index check, $O(1)$) with zero need for complex matrix calculations, maximizing throughput at the cost of requiring programmers to strictly obey lock ordering protocols. Embedded Medical Device: Deadlock Avoidance via Banker's Algorithm System Characteristics: Life-critical reliability, bounded number of tasks/actuators (e.g., infusion pump, heart monitor), zero tolerance for task termination or data loss. Why Banker's Algorithm: In embedded systems, the task set is static and the maximum resource requirements of each hardware driver and thread are fully known at compile time. Avoidance ensures the system never transitions into an unsafe state, completely preventing deadlock without forcing rigid static acquisition sequences. Trade-Off Assessment: The $O(M \times N^2)$ computational overhead of matrix evaluation is completely negligible because $N$ and $M$ are small, while preserving 100% execution safety without

ever aborting a life-critical process. Comparison Summary: Criterion Bank (Deadlock Prevention) Medical Device (Deadlock Avoidance) Primary Objective High transaction throughput & low latency. Deterministic execution safety; zero aborted tasks. A Priori Knowledge None required for dynamic accounts. Maximum resource claims known at compile time. Runtime Overhead Negligible ($O(1)$ lock ordering check). Moderate matrix checking ($O(M \times N^2)$), acceptable for small $N$.
subject: os

title: Critically analyze why Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm) is theoretically stronger than Deadlock Prevention but is rarely used in real operating systems, with reference to the assumption that maximum resource needs must be known in advance.
chunks: Critical Analysis of Deadlock Avoidance vs. Deadlock Prevention in Practical Operating Systems: Theoretical Superiority of Avoidance: Theoretically, Deadlock Avoidance (e.g., Banker's Algorithm) is vastly superior to Deadlock Prevention because it does not impose artificial, restrictive constraints on resource usage (such as holding only one resource, releasing all resources, or enforcing rigid linear acquisition order). It dynamically grants requests as long as the system remains in a safe state, maximizing resource flexibility and concurrency. The Fatal Assumption: Advance Knowledge of Maximum Resource Needs The Banker's Algorithm requires every process to declare its maximum resource claim a priori before execution starts. In modern general-purpose operating systems (Linux, Windows, macOS), applications are inherently dynamic, event-driven, and user-interactive. A web browser, software compiler, or text editor cannot predict how many memory pages, file handles, or network sockets it will allocate because resource demands depend entirely on runtime user input, web page complexity, and dynamic memory allocations. If an application conservatively overestimates its maximum claim, the OS unnecessarily denies resource requests to other processes, causing severe artificial resource starvation. Static Process and Resource Assumptions: The Banker's Algorithm assumes a fixed number of processes ($N$) and a fixed number of resources ($M$). In real OS environments,

processes constantly fork, spawn threads, and terminate, while peripheral resources (printers, USB storage, network adapters) are hot-plugged and unplugged dynamically. Runtime Computational Overhead: Running the safety algorithm ($O(M \times N^2)$) on every single resource request or memory frame allocation introduces prohibitive CPU latency bottlenecks on multi-core systems running thousands of threads. Pragmatic Conclusion: Because real applications cannot accurately pre-declare maximum demands, general-purpose operating systems abandon avoidance in favor of the Ostrich Algorithm combined with lightweight user-space timeouts, lock ranking (prevention), or manual process termination via task managers.

title: Define Virtual Memory.
chunks: Virtual Memory is a memory management technique that separates user logical memory from physical memory (RAM), allowing the execution of processes that may not be completely loaded into physical storage. Core Benefit: Allows logical address space to be significantly larger than physical RAM, maximizing multiprogramming capacity. Mechanism: Implemented via Demand Paging or Demand Segmentation backed by secondary swap storage.
subject: os

title: What is a Page Fault?
chunks: A Page Fault is a hardware interrupt (trap) generated by the Memory Management Unit (MMU) when an executing process attempts to access a virtual page whose valid-invalid bit in the page table is set to 0 (invalid), indicating it is not currently resident in physical RAM. Resolution: The OS traps into kernel mode, retrieves the missing page from secondary storage (swap/disk), loads it into a physical frame, updates the page table bit to valid ( 1 ), and restarts the trapped instruction.
subject: os

title: Define Thrashing.
chunks: Thrashing is a severe operating state where a computer spends substantially more time swapping pages between main memory and secondary storage (paging I/O) than executing actual application instructions. Cause: Occurs when the sum of the working sets of active processes exceeds total available physical frames ($\sum \text{WSS}_i > D$). Symptom: Disk queue saturation accompanied by a sharp collapse in CPU utilization toward zero.
subject: os

title: Differentiate between Virtual Memory and Physical Memory on the basis of speed and volatility.
chunks: Criterion Virtual Memory Physical Memory (RAM) Access Speed Slow: Non-resident page accesses require disk/SSD paging I/O, incurring mechanical/bus latency in milliseconds ($10\text{--}100\text{ ms}$) or microseconds. Fast: Directly accessed by the CPU via hardware memory buses with nanosecond cycle times ($10\text{--}100\text{ ns}$). Volatility Persistent Backing: Stored on magnetic disks or NVMe SSD swap partitions, surviving power interruptions (though page table mappings are volatile). Strictly Volatile: Relies on electrical capacitance (DRAM); all stored data is permanently lost upon system shutdown or power loss.

title: What is the difference between Global Replacement and Local Replacement frame allocation?
chunks: Feature Global Replacement Local Replacement Victim Selection A faulting process can select a replacement victim frame from the set of all frames , preempting frames owned by other processes. A faulting process is strictly restricted to selecting a replacement victim frame from its own allocated pool of frames. System Impact Yields higher system throughput, but individual process execution times are unpredictable and prone to cascading thrashing. Guarantees consistent per-process runtime isolation and confines thrashing, but cannot dynamically adapt if unused frames remain idle elsewhere.

title: Differentiate between Sequential Access and Direct Access file access methods.
chunks: Feature Sequential Access Direct (Random) Access Access Order Information in the file is processed strictly in order, one record after the other (from start to finish). Reaching record $N$ requires traversing records $1$ to $N-1$. Blocks or records can be read or written immediately in any arbitrary sequence using a relative block number (e.g., via lseek() ) without sequential scanning. Use Case Compilers, editors, log files, and magnetic tape streaming where files are read in linear order. Relational databases, indexing structures, and airline reservation systems requiring instant record retrieval.

title: A process requires 10 GB but the main memory is only 4 GB. Explain which memory management technique allows this process to still execute, and how.
chunks: The technique that enables this execution is Virtual Memory with Demand Paging . How it operates: The operating system splits the process's 10 GB logical address space into fixed-size pages and maintains them on secondary storage (swap/pagefile). Physical RAM (4 GB) acts as an active frame cache. Execution Mechanism: Only the immediate working set of instructions and data is resident in the 4 GB RAM. As the CPU executes, non-resident pages trigger demand page faults, dynamically swapping requested pages into memory and evicting inactive frames using replacement algorithms.

title: In a Bit Vector used for free space management, a block's bit value changes from 1 to 0 after an operation. Identify which operation (allocation or deallocation) just occurred.
chunks: The operation that just occurred is Block Allocation . Bit Vector Convention: In standard operating system design (e.g., Silberschatz), a bit value of 1 signifies that the corresponding disk block is free (available) , while 0 signifies that the block is allocated (occupied) . Transition: When a file system allocates a free block ($1$) to store file data, it flips the corresponding bit to $0$ to indicate that the block is now reserved and unavailable for subsequent requests.

title: A disk's read/write head is at track 50 and receives a request for track 82. Name the disk access time component responsible for the head physically moving from track 50 to track 82.
chunks: The component responsible is Seek Time . Definition: Seek time is the physical duration required for the disk actuator arm to move the read/write head assembly radially across the platter cylinders from its current position (track 50) to the destination cylinder (track 82). Significance: Seek time constitutes the largest and most latency-intensive mechanical component of disk access time (typically $3\text{--}10\text{ ms}$).
subject: os

title: A system shows a sudden drop in CPU utilization even though the degree of multiprogramming has increased. Identify the phenomenon responsible, and briefly explain why increasing multiprogramming further would worsen it.
chunks: The phenomenon is Thrashing . Why further multiprogramming worsens it: When multiprogramming exceeds memory capacity, allocated frames per process drop below their minimum working sets, causing continuous page faults and queuing on the swap disk. The Vicious Cycle: The CPU scheduler perceives low CPU utilization as system underload and admits more processes to the ready queue. These new processes steal frames from existing ones, accelerating page fault rates and driving CPU utilization down toward zero.

title: Explain the steps involved in handling a Page Fault.
chunks: When a process references an invalid page table entry, the OS handles the page fault through the following systematic sequence: Trap to OS: The MMU detects an invalid bit reference and triggers an internal hardware trap to the OS kernel. Validate Reference: The OS saves user registers and checks the Process Control Block (PCB). If the address is invalid, the process is terminated (Segmentation Fault); otherwise, it proceeds with paging. Locate on Backing Store: The OS determines the physical disk address of the missing page on the swap device. Allocate Physical Frame: The OS finds a free frame from the free-frame list. If none are free, a page replacement algorithm (e.g., LRU) selects a victim frame, writing it back to disk if modified (dirty bit set). Disk I/O: A disk read request is scheduled to fetch the requested page into the selected frame; the faulting process enters the I/O wait queue. Update Page Table & Restart: Upon I/O completion interrupt, the OS updates the page table (sets frame number, valid bit to 1 ), restores process registers, and restarts the instruction.

title: List and briefly explain any three types of Frame Allocation.
chunks: Operating systems allocate available physical memory frames to competing processes using several primary strategies: 1. Equal Allocation: All $m$ available frames are divided equally among $n$ processes: $a_i = \lfloor m / n \rfloor$. While straightforward, it is inefficient because small utility processes receive excess frames while large database applications starve. 2. Proportional Allocation: Frames are allocated proportionally according to the virtual address space size ($s_i$) of each process relative to total memory demands ($S = \sum s_i$): $$a_i = \left\lfloor \frac{s_i}{S} \times m \right\rfloor$$ Large processes receive more frames, balancing fault rates across uneven process sizes. 3. Priority Allocation: Frame distribution is guided by process execution priority rather than size alone. Higher-priority processes receive larger frame quotas (or can preempt frames from lower-priority processes during page faults) to ensure predictable real-time response.
subject: os

title: Explain the three components of disk access time: Seek Time, Rotational Latency, and Transfer Time.
chunks: Total disk access time represents the cumulative latency required to service a disk read or write request: $T_{\text{access}} = T_{\text{seek}} + T_{\text{rotational}} + T_{\text{transfer}}$. 1. Seek Time ($T_{\text{seek}}$): The mechanical delay required for the disk actuator arm to move the read/write head assembly radially to the cylinder/track containing the target sector (typically $3\text{--}9\text{ ms}$). 2. Rotational Latency ($T_{\text{rotational}}$): The time waiting for the target sector on the rotating platter to rotate directly beneath the read/write head. Average rotational latency is the time for half a platter revolution: $$T_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2 \times \text{RPM}} \times 60\text{ s}$$ (e.g., $4.17\text{ ms}$ at 7200 RPM). 3. Transfer Time ($T_{\text{transfer}}$): The time required to physically stream data bits between the magnetic disk surface and the disk controller buffer: $$T_{\text{trans}} = \frac{\text{Bytes to Transfer}}{\text{Transfer Rate}}$$
subject: os

title: Differentiate between FIFO and LRU page replacement algorithms.
chunks: Comparison Feature First-In, First-Out (FIFO) Least Recently Used (LRU) Eviction Rule Evicts the page that has resided in physical memory the longest, regardless of recent usage. Evicts the page that has not been referenced for the longest duration in the past. Implementation Overhead Low: Maintained via a simple FIFO queue or circular pointer; no updates needed on page hits. High: Requires hardware support (logical timestamps or a doubly linked reference stack) updated on every single memory hit. Belady's Anomaly Susceptible: Allocating more page frames can paradoxically increase total page faults. Immune: Belonging to the class of stack algorithms ($M(n) \subseteq M(n+1)$), increasing frames never increases faults. Performance Often evicts heavily used global variables or core loops, yielding sub-optimal hit ratios. Closely approximates the theoretical optimal algorithm by effectively exploiting temporal locality.

title: Compare Linked Allocation and Indexed Allocation methods of file allocation on the basis of random access and fragmentation.
chunks: Evaluation Criterion Linked Allocation Indexed Allocation Random (Direct) Access Extremely Inefficient: Each block contains a pointer to the next block. Accessing block $i$ requires following $i$ pointers sequentially from the start of the file ($O(i)$ disk seeks). Highly Efficient: Direct access is supported ($O(1)$ disk seeks) by looking up block $i$'s pointer directly in the $i$-th entry of the dedicated index block. Internal Fragmentation Minimal: Restricted solely to the final partially filled data block of the file. Minimal: Confined to the last data block, plus slight unused entry space in the index block. External Fragmentation None: Any available free disk block can be linked into any file anywhere on disk. None: Blocks are scattered arbitrarily across the disk and aggregated via the index block. Storage Overhead Pointer overhead within every data block (e.g., 4 or 8 bytes per 512-byte block lost to pointers). Requires an entire dedicated disk block (index block) per file, creating noticeable overhead for very small files.

title: Differentiate between Single-Level Directory and Two-Level Directory structures.
chunks: Comparison Dimension Single-Level Directory Two-Level Directory Hierarchy A single flat directory contains all files for all users in the system. A Master File Directory (MFD) indexes separate User File Directories (UFDs) for each user. Naming Collisions Severe: All filenames must be globally unique across all users; two users cannot name a file main.c . Eliminated: Different users can have identical filenames because files are scoped within their distinct UFD (e.g., /user1/main.c vs /user2/main.c ). User Isolation No user isolation; access control and privacy between users are difficult to enforce. Natural user isolation; provides defined pathnames and straightforward per-user access control. File Grouping No sub-grouping of files is possible. Files are organized by user, though sub-grouping within an individual account is still absent.

title: A disk has 4 platters. Each surface has 15 tracks, and each track has 40 sectors of 512 bytes. Calculate the total number of surfaces on the disk and the total storage capacity of the disk in bytes.
chunks: Given Parameters: Number of platters = 4 Tracks per surface = 15 Sectors per track = 40 Bytes per sector = 512 bytes Step 1: Total Number of Surfaces Each platter has 2 recording surfaces (top and bottom): $$\text{Total Surfaces} = \text{Platters} \times 2 = 4 \times 2 = \mathbf{8\text{ surfaces}}$$ Step 2: Total Storage Capacity Calculation $$\text{Total Capacity} = \text{Surfaces} \times \text{Tracks per Surface} \times \text{Sectors per Track} \times \text{Bytes per Sector}$$ $$\text{Total Capacity} = 8 \times 15 \times 40 \times 512\text{ bytes}$$ $$\text{Total Tracks} = 8 \times 15 = 120\text{ tracks}$$ $$\text{Total Sectors} = 120 \times 40 = 4{,}800\text{ sectors}$$ $$\text{Total Capacity} = 4{,}800 \times 512 = \mathbf{2{,}457{,}600\text{ bytes}}$$ In Kibibytes / Mebibytes: $$2{,}457{,}600\text{ bytes} = 2{,}400\text{ KiB} = 2.34375\text{ MiB}$$

title: A file system uses Discretionary Access Control (DAC), where a user creates a file and grants read access to all other users. Identify the access control model in use, and explain one risk of this approach.
chunks: Access Control Model: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) . Core Principle: In DAC, the creator/owner of an object has complete discretion to grant, modify, or revoke permissions (Read/Write/Execute) to other subjects using Access Control Lists (ACLs) or permission bits (e.g., UNIX chmod ). Major Risk — Uncontrolled Propagation & Trojan Horses: DAC lacks transitive information flow control. If User A grants read access to User B, User B can easily copy the contents into a new file owned by User B and publish it publicly to everyone. Furthermore, malicious Trojan horse programs executing under a privileged user's identity can silently reconfigure ACLs, leaking confidential data without triggering access violations.

title: Explain why the Working Set Model and Page Fault Frequency (PFF) control are both used to prevent Thrashing, describing how each approach detects a process that needs more frames.
chunks: Both techniques prevent thrashing by ensuring processes receive their essential working frame requirements before memory overcommitment triggers systemic collapse: 1. Working Set Model (Locality-Based): Concept: Based on Peter Denning's locality model, the working set $W(t, \Delta)$ comprises all pages referenced within the most recent $\Delta$ page references (working set window). Detection: The OS tracks the working set size $\text{WSS}_i$ of each process. It calculates total memory demand $D = \sum \text{WSS}_i$. If $D > m$ (available physical frames), thrashing is imminent. The OS detects processes whose allocated frames $< \text{WSS}_i$ and suspends/swaps out processes until $D \le m$. 2. Page Fault Frequency (PFF) Control (Rate-Based): Concept: Directly measures the empirical page fault rate of each process against fixed upper and lower fault thresholds ($TR_{\text{high}}$ and $TR_{\text{low}}$). Detection: If a process's page fault rate rises above $TR_{\text{high}}$, it lacks sufficient frames to hold its active working set; the OS grants it additional frames. If the fault rate falls below $TR_{\text{low}}$, the process has surplus frames, which the OS safely reclaims. If free frames are exhausted and fault rates remain high, a process is suspended.
subject: os

title: Explain the FIFO, Optimal, and LRU page replacement algorithms, describing the basic working principle of each.
chunks: Page replacement algorithms manage virtual memory frames when no free frame is available during a page fault. The three foundational algorithms are: First-In, First-Out (FIFO) Algorithm: Working Principle: Associates each page with the timestamp or queue position when it entered physical memory. When a replacement is required, the page that has been in memory the longest is evicted. Implementation: Maintained via a simple FIFO queue where incoming pages are enqueued at the tail and victim pages are dequeued from the head. Limitation: Suffers from Belady's Anomaly , where allocating more physical frames can paradoxically increase the number of page faults. It frequently evicts heavily referenced initialization pages or global data. Optimal (OPT / MIN) Algorithm: Working Principle: The theoretical gold standard. Evicts the page that will not be referenced for the longest period of time in the future . Implementation: Requires clairvoyant knowledge of future memory reference strings; therefore, it cannot be implemented in general-purpose operating systems. Significance: Serves as an unassailable benchmark against which all practical page replacement algorithms are measured. Least Recently Used (LRU) Algorithm: Working Principle: Exploits the principle of temporal locality (recent past references predict near-future behavior). Evicts the page that has not been referenced for

the longest period in the past . Implementation: Requires hardware support: either per-entry access counters/timers or a doubly linked reference stack where referenced page numbers are pulled to the top. Characteristics: Highly efficient and immune to Belady's Anomaly (belongs to the family of stack algorithms where $M(n) \subseteq M(n+1)$). Algorithm Basis of Replacement Implementation Cost Belady's Anomaly FIFO Oldest resident page Very low (queue) Yes Optimal Furthest future reference Unrealizable (ideal benchmark) No LRU Longest time since last access High (counters / hardware stack) No

title: Explain Thrashing — its causes and the methods used to prevent it.
chunks: Thrashing is a pathological system condition in virtual memory management where an operating system spends virtually all its resources servicing page faults (swapping pages between memory and disk) rather than executing productive process instructions, causing CPU utilization to plummet toward zero. Primary Causes of Thrashing: Overcommitment of Multiprogramming: When the OS scheduler admits too many processes into memory, the number of frames allocated to each process drops below its minimum working set. Global Page Replacement Policy: When process $A$ page faults, it can steal a frame from process $B$. Process $B$ immediately page faults and steals a frame from process $C$, propagating a cascading chain reaction of page faults across the entire system. Violation of Locality: If a process transitions to a new execution phase where its working set demand exceeds its allocated frames, frequent page faults saturate the swap disk queue. Methods to Prevent Thrashing: Working Set Model (Peter Denning): Defines the working set $W(t, \Delta)$ as the set of pages referenced in the most recent $\Delta$ time units. The OS computes working set size $\text{WSS}_i$ for each process and total frame demand $D = \sum \text{WSS}_i$. If $D > m$ (total physical frames), thrashing is imminent. The OS

suspends (swaps out) one or more processes and reallocates their frames to active processes until $D \le m$. Page Fault Frequency (PFF) Strategy: Establishes upper ($TR_{\text{high}}$) and lower ($TR_{\text{low}}$) acceptable page fault rate boundaries. If a process's page fault rate exceeds $TR_{\text{high}}$, it is allocated additional frames. If its rate falls below $TR_{\text{low}}$, excess frames are reclaimed. If page faults remain high across processes and no free frames exist, the OS swaps out an entire process to free up physical memory. Local Page Replacement Policy: Forces each process to select replacement frames strictly from its own allocated frame pool, isolating thrashing to offending processes and preventing system-wide collapse.
subject: os

title: Explain the four types of Directory Structures — Single-Level, Two-Level, Tree-Structured, and Acyclic-Graph — with one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
chunks: Operating systems organize files using distinct directory structures, balancing naming flexibility, protection, and sharing: Single-Level Directory: Structure: A single global directory containing all files created by all users in the entire system. Advantage: Very simple to implement and requires minimal directory lookup overhead. Disadvantage: Severe naming collision problems (all filenames across all users must be globally unique) and zero logical grouping or user protection. Two-Level Directory: Structure: A Master File Directory (MFD) points to separate User File Directories (UFDs) for each user account. Advantage: Eliminates inter-user naming collisions (different users can have files with identical names, e.g., /userA/lab.c and /userB/lab.c ). Disadvantage: Lacks sub-grouping capabilities within individual user accounts; file sharing between different users remains difficult. Tree-Structured Directory: Structure: Generalization to an arbitrary tree hierarchy with a root directory, user directories, subdirectories, and files. Advantage: Highly flexible logical organization and grouping; supports absolute and relative pathnames. Disadvantage: Cannot share files across distinct directory branches without physical data duplication (no shared references). Acyclic-Graph Directory: Structure: An extension of tree directories allowing directories to share subdirectories and files via links/aliases without cycles. Advantage: Facilitates seamless file sharing and collaborative editing across multiple users using hard or symbolic links. Disadvantage: Complex deletion semantics (dangling pointers or reference-counting overhead) and risk of cycle creation during link additions.
subject: os

title: Compare Contiguous, Linked, and Indexed File Allocation methods on the basis of fragmentation, access speed, and overhead.
chunks: File allocation determines how secondary storage blocks are assigned to files. The three primary methods compare as follows: Evaluation Criterion Contiguous Allocation Linked Allocation Indexed Allocation Storage Principle Each file occupies a set of consecutive disk blocks on adjacent cylinders. Each file is a linked list of scattered disk blocks; each block contains a pointer to the next block. Each file possesses a dedicated index block containing an array of pointers to all its scattered data blocks. External Fragmentation Severe: Free space gets fragmented into small holes; requires periodic offline disk compaction. None: Any available free block anywhere on disk can be chained into a file. None: Any available block can be assigned and recorded in the index block. Internal Fragmentation Only in the last partially filled block of the file. Only in the last partially filled block of the file. In the last data block, plus unused pointer space in the index block. Access Speed (Sequential) Extremely Fast: Minimal disk head movement due to contiguous sector layout. Moderate: Requires sequential pointer traversal; seeks may jump across disk platters. Fast: Pointers are cached in memory from the index block. Access Speed (Direct/Random) Instant ($O(1)$): Block $k$ is located at $\text{start}

+ k$. Very Slow ($O(k)$): Must sequentially traverse $k-1$ disk blocks to reach block $k$. Instant ($O(1)$): Direct index lookup via the $k$-th pointer in the index block. Metadata Overhead Minimal: Directory entry stores only starting block number and length. Low-to-Moderate: Pointers consume 4--8 bytes per data block (lost payload). Moderate-to-High: Requires an entire dedicated disk block per file, even for tiny files. Dynamic Growth Difficult: File cannot grow beyond pre-allocated size without relocating entire file. Trivial: New blocks are simply appended to the linked list tail. Trivial: Pointers added to index block (multi-level indexing used for very large files).

title: Explain Discretionary Access Control (DAC) and Mandatory Access Control (MAC), comparing their working, security level, and typical use cases.
chunks: Access control models define how an operating system regulates subject (user/process) access to objects (files/devices): Discretionary Access Control (DAC): Working Principle: The creator/owner of a file has complete discretion over permission assignment. The owner explicitly defines access privileges (Read, Write, Execute) for specific users or groups via Access Control Lists (ACLs) or permission bits (e.g., POSIX chmod/chown ). Security Level: Moderate to Low . DAC cannot prevent transitive data leakage or Trojan horses: if User A authorizes User B to read a secret file, User B can copy the contents into a new file and grant read access to everyone. Typical Use Cases: General-purpose commercial operating systems (standard Linux, macOS, Microsoft Windows NTFS). Mandatory Access Control (MAC): Working Principle: Access decisions are centrally enforced by the operating system kernel based on fixed, system-wide security policies. Every subject is assigned a clearance label , and every object is assigned a classification label (e.g., Unclassified, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret). Users cannot alter or delegate permissions. Security Rules: Enforces mathematical security models such as the Bell-LaPadula model : Simple Security Property (No Read Up): A subject at a lower clearance level cannot read an object at a higher classification level. $\star$-Property (No Write Down): A subject at a higher clearance level cannot write/leak information into an object at a lower classification level. Security Level: High . Immune to Trojan horses and unauthorized delegation. Typical Use Cases: Military, defense systems, intelligence agencies, high-assurance banking, and SELinux / TrustedBSD environments.
subject: os

title: Compare any four Disk Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK) in terms of total head movement and fairness.
chunks: Disk scheduling algorithms optimize the order in which I/O requests for disk tracks are serviced, balancing seek performance against process fairness. A comparison of four core algorithms follows: Algorithm Working Principle Total Head Movement Fairness & Starvation Risk FCFS (First-Come, First-Served) Services disk requests strictly in the order of their arrival in the I/O queue. Worst (Highest): Incurs massive, wild head swings across distant platters when requests are scattered. Completely Fair: Every request is guaranteed service in arrival order; zero starvation risk. SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) Selects the pending request with the minimum seek distance from the current head position. Substantially Lower: Dramatically reduces total seek distance compared to FCFS. Unfair: High starvation risk. A continuous stream of nearby requests can starve distant cylinder requests indefinitely. SCAN (Elevator) The disk arm moves in one direction servicing all requests until it reaches the physical end of the disk, then reverses direction. Moderate / Good: Provides efficient seek clustering and bounded head travel. Fair: Prevents starvation. However, tracks just visited experience longer wait times than middle cylinders. C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) The disk arm moves in one direction servicing requests to the end, then immediately returns to the beginning without servicing requests on the return trip. Slightly higher than SCAN due to the full return sweep, but highly predictable. Extremely Fair: Provides uniform waiting time distribution across all cylinders by treating cylinders as a circular list.
subject: os

title: Consider the following disk scheduling scenario: Disk Request Queue: 55, 58, 39, 18, 90, 160, 150, 38, 184; Current Head Position: 100. Using a disk having 200 tracks (0–199), calculate the total head movement using (a) the FCFS disk scheduling algorithm and (b) the SSTF disk scheduling algorithm. Show the order of track service for each.
chunks: Given Parameters: Disk Request Queue: 55, 58, 39, 18, 90, 160, 150, 38, 184 Current Head Position: 100 Total tracks: 200 ($0\text{ to }199$)

title: Using the Working Set Model, a newly started process has not yet built up its working set and is experiencing excessive page faults. Explain why Minimum Frame Allocation would help this process, and what happens if the OS fails to provide it.
chunks: The Cold-Start Dilemma: When a process begins execution, its working set window contains zero resident pages. Every initial memory reference triggers a cold-start page fault. Until the process populates its working set $W(t, \Delta)$ with essential code segments, stack frames, and globals, it experiences high fault frequencies. Why Minimum Frame Allocation Helps: Instruction Completion Guarantee: CPU machine architectures require that certain multi-byte or complex instructions execute atomically. For example, an indirect addressing instruction like MOVE (R1)+, (R2)+ may require up to 6 distinct frames simultaneously: the instruction page, indirect source address page, actual source page, indirect destination address page, destination page, and stack pointer. Preventing Intra-Instruction Thrashing: Minimum frame allocation guarantees that an executing instruction can hold all required pages in physical memory simultaneously, ensuring execution progresses without getting trapped in a page-fault cycle mid-instruction. What Happens if the OS Fails to Provide Minimum Frames: Infinite Trap Loops: If a process receives fewer frames than required by a single instruction, it will fetch page $A$, fault on page $B$, evict page $A$ to load $B$, restart the instruction, fault on page $A$ again, and evict page $B$—trapping the CPU in an endless, unresolvable page-fault loop. Severe Process Starvation: The process can never complete a single clock cycle of productive work, starving indefinitely in the wait queue. Immediate Thrashing: The CPU scheduler repeatedly cycles through unexecutable threads, driving paging disk queues to $100\%$ saturation.

title: A hospital database system uses Indexed File Allocation for patient records (which need both direct and sequential access), while a video streaming service uses Linked Allocation for sequential video segments. Justify why each system chose its respective file allocation method, based on the characteristics of indexed versus linked allocation.
chunks: The choice of file allocation method is fundamentally dictated by access pattern requirements and metadata overhead trade-offs: Hospital Database System $\rightarrow$ Indexed File Allocation: Instant Direct Access ($O(1)$): Medical emergencies require immediate retrieval of patient records by Patient ID or record number. Indexed allocation stores all block pointers in an index block, allowing direct address calculation in $O(1)$ disk seeks without scanning preceding records. Efficient Sequential Reporting: The index block maintains ordered block pointers, allowing linear reading of records for audits and daily ward reports without fragmentation. Dynamic Record Expansion: Patient files grow unpredictably with test results and scans. Indexed allocation easily accommodates new blocks by inserting pointers into the index block without relocating the entire file or causing external fragmentation. Video Streaming Service $\rightarrow$ Linked Allocation: Pure Sequential Streaming Pipeline: Video media is streamed and consumed sequentially from start to finish. Traversing block pointers ($O(n)$) has zero latency penalty because playback naturally processes block $k$ after $k-1$ in a continuous stream buffer. Zero Index Overhead for Large Media: Massive video files (several gigabytes) would require massive multi-level index blocks under indexed allocation, wasting RAM and disk space. Linked allocation incurs zero dedicated index block overhead. Optimal Storage Utilization: Continuous

4K/8K media chunks can be assigned any scattered free blocks across high-capacity disk arrays with zero external fragmentation. Workload Requirement Hospital Database Video Streaming Service Primary Access Pattern Random/Direct (Emergency lookups) & Sequential Strictly Sequential (Streaming pipeline) Preferred Allocation Indexed Allocation Linked Allocation Decisive Factor $O(1)$ random access via index pointers Zero index overhead; smooth sequential chaining

title: Critically analyze the trade-off between Global Replacement and Local Replacement frame allocation policies, explaining why Global Replacement can give better overall throughput but cause unpredictable performance for individual processes, using the concept of Thrashing to support your answer.
chunks: The conflict between Global Replacement and Local Replacement represents a classic operating systems trade-off between aggregate system throughput and individual process execution predictability: 1. Why Global Replacement Achieves Higher Overall Throughput: Dynamic Resource Adaptation: Processes have constantly shifting working set sizes. Global replacement dynamically shifts memory frames from idle or sleeping processes to active, compute-heavy processes. Minimized Unused Frame Waste: No physical frames remain locked or underutilized in static process allocations. This optimal utilization maximizes overall system throughput under light-to-moderate workloads. 2. Why Global Replacement Causes Unpredictable Performance & Cascading Thrashing: Loss of Per-Process Runtime Isolation: Under global replacement, a process's paging behavior is not independent—it depends on the memory access patterns of every other active process in the system. A process may run in 5 seconds in one instance and 5 minutes in another. Cascading Thrashing Contagion: If one rogue or memory-intensive process starts thrashing, it continuously page faults and preempts frames from other well-behaved processes. The victim processes, now stripped of their working sets, immediately begin page faulting as well and steal frames from others. System-Wide Collapse: This triggers a domino effect of page faults across all processes, saturating the paging disk queues and driving CPU utilization to

near zero. 3. The Local Replacement Trade-off: Containment of Thrashing: Local replacement restricts victim selection strictly to the faulting process's own allocated frame pool. If a process thrashes, the blast radius is strictly contained to that single process, ensuring other processes continue executing with predictable runtimes. Drawback: It cannot reclaim unreferenced frames from processes that have completed a phase, leading to lower overall memory efficiency and throughput. Conclusion: Modern operating systems employ hybrid strategies (such as PFF or the Working Set Model with local replacement fallbacks) to capture the throughput benefits of global allocation while enforcing dynamic quotas that prevent catastrophic thrashing contagion.
